definition: Impossible to avoid, resist, or escape.
etymology: From Latin ineluctabilis, from in- 'not' plus eluctari 'to struggle out,' from luctari 'to wrestle.'
exampleSentence: There was an ineluctable sadness in the way he closed the door for the last time.

definition: A person who flatters powerful people to gain advantage.
etymology: From Greek sykophantes, originally 'fig-shower,' an informer against people who illegally exported figs, later 'slanderer' and 'flatterer.'
exampleSentence: The new CEO surrounded himself with sycophants who agreed with everything he said.

definition: Having keen insight and understanding of things.
etymology: From Latin perspicax 'sharp-sighted,' from perspicere 'to look through, see clearly.'
exampleSentence: Her perspicacious comments cut through the noise of the meeting.

definition: Composure or coolness under stress or danger.
etymology: From French sang-froid, literally 'cold blood,' adopted into English in the eighteenth century.
exampleSentence: He handled the heckler with the sangfroid of a seasoned comedian.

definition: Excessively eager to please or obey.
etymology: From Latin obsequiosus, from obsequium 'compliance,' from obsequi 'to follow, comply with.'
exampleSentence: The waiter's obsequious manner made the meal feel oddly uncomfortable.

definition: Looking or sounding sad and dismal, often comically so.
etymology: From Latin lugubris 'mournful,' from lugere 'to mourn.'
exampleSentence: He gave a lugubrious sigh and reached for another slice of cake.

definition: The appearance of being true or real.
etymology: From Latin verisimilitudo, from verisimilis 'probable,' from veri 'true' plus similis 'like.'
exampleSentence: The novel's verisimilitude comes from years of meticulous research.

definition: Stubbornly resistant to authority or control.
etymology: From Latin recalcitrare 'to kick back,' from re- plus calcitrare 'to kick,' from calx 'heel.'
exampleSentence: My recalcitrant printer chose this morning, of all mornings, to jam.

definition: Habitually dishonest or untruthful.
etymology: From Latin mendax 'lying,' related to mendum 'fault, defect.'
exampleSentence: His mendacious testimony fell apart under cross-examination.

definition: Very attentive to detail and easily disgusted by mess.
etymology: From Latin fastidiosus 'disdainful,' from fastidium 'loathing.'
exampleSentence: She was so fastidious about her sourdough starter that it had its own thermometer.

definition: Something reused but bearing visible traces of its earlier form.
etymology: From Greek palimpsestos 'scraped again,' from palin 'again' plus psen 'to rub smooth.'
exampleSentence: The old neighborhood is a palimpsest of immigrant histories layered atop one another.

definition: Of doubtful authenticity, though widely told.
etymology: From Greek apokryphos 'hidden,' from apokryptein 'to hide away.'
exampleSentence: The story about Einstein failing math is apocryphal but charming.

definition: The final resolution of a story or sequence of events.
etymology: From French denouement 'an untying,' from desnouer 'to untie,' from Latin nodus 'knot.'
exampleSentence: After three seasons of buildup, the show's denouement felt rushed.

definition: A feeling of listless boredom and dissatisfaction.
etymology: From French ennui 'annoyance,' from Old French enui, ultimately from Latin in odio 'in hatred.'
exampleSentence: By July, an ennui had settled over the office like a heavy curtain.

definition: Having a harmful effect, especially in a gradual or subtle way.
etymology: From Latin perniciosus, from pernicies 'destruction,' from per- plus nex 'death.'
exampleSentence: The pernicious influence of constant comparison gnaws at self-esteem.

definition: Eager or quick to argue or fight.
etymology: From Latin truculentus 'fierce,' from trux 'fierce, savage.'
exampleSentence: The truculent customer demanded to see the manager before even ordering.

definition: Lacking a plan or purpose; jumping randomly between things.
etymology: From Latin desultorius 'pertaining to a vaulter,' from desultor, a circus rider who leapt between horses.
exampleSentence: They made desultory small talk while waiting for the elevator.

definition: Lasting only a very short time.
etymology: From Greek ephemeros 'lasting only a day,' from epi- 'on' plus hemera 'day.'
exampleSentence: Cherry blossoms are beautiful precisely because they are ephemeral.

definition: Difficult to understand; dealing with very obscure subject matter.
etymology: From Latin reconditus 'hidden away,' past participle of recondere 'to put away.'
exampleSentence: His dissertation on medieval taxation was admirably recondite.

definition: Physical beauty.
etymology: From Latin pulchritudo, from pulcher 'beautiful.'
exampleSentence: The valley's pulchritude was the kind that silenced even chatty tourists.

definition: Of such excellence or beauty as to inspire awe.
etymology: From Latin sublimis 'lofty, elevated,' possibly from sub- 'up to' plus limen 'threshold, lintel.'
exampleSentence: The first bite of that pastry was, frankly, sublime.

definition: Clear, logical, and convincing.
etymology: From Latin cogens, present participle of cogere 'to compel,' from co- plus agere 'to drive.'
exampleSentence: She made a cogent argument for working from home three days a week.

definition: Deceitful and untrustworthy.
etymology: From Latin perfidiosus, from perfidia 'faithlessness,' from per- plus fides 'faith.'
exampleSentence: His perfidious double-dealing eventually cost him every friend he had.

definition: Noisy and unruly, especially in resisting control.
etymology: From Latin obstreperus, from obstrepere 'to make a noise against,' from ob- plus strepere 'to make a noise.'
exampleSentence: An obstreperous toddler dominated the otherwise quiet cafe.

definition: Given to using long words.
etymology: From Latin sesquipedalis 'a foot and a half long,' coined by Horace to mock pompous diction.
exampleSentence: His sesquipedalian style charmed academics and alienated everyone else.

definition: Calm and unemotional, especially under pressure.
etymology: From Greek phlegmatikos, referring to the bodily humor phlegm thought to produce a stolid temperament.
exampleSentence: Her phlegmatic response to the fire alarm reassured the children.

definition: Wanting or consuming great amounts, especially of food or information.
etymology: From Latin vorax 'greedy,' from vorare 'to devour.'
exampleSentence: He was a voracious reader who finished two novels every week.

definition: Shining brilliantly; radiant.
etymology: From Latin effulgens, present participle of effulgere 'to shine forth,' from ex- plus fulgere 'to shine.'
exampleSentence: The effulgent sunset turned the lake into molten copper.

definition: A supposed cure-all for problems or diseases.
etymology: From Greek panakeia, from pan 'all' plus akos 'remedy,' originally the name of a healing goddess.
exampleSentence: Don't treat any single app as a panacea for productivity.

definition: Tending to disappear quickly; fleeting.
etymology: From Latin fugax 'apt to flee,' from fugere 'to flee.'
exampleSentence: The morning's optimism proved fugacious once the news came in.

definition: To criticize severely.
etymology: From Latin excoriatus, past participle of excoriare 'to strip the skin off,' from ex- plus corium 'hide.'
exampleSentence: Critics excoriated the sequel for repeating every flaw of the original.

definition: To waver between different opinions or actions.
etymology: From Latin vacillatus, past participle of vacillare 'to sway.'
exampleSentence: He vacillated for weeks before finally accepting the job offer.

definition: To clear someone of blame or fault.
etymology: From Medieval Latin exculpatus, from ex- 'out of' plus culpa 'fault, blame.'
exampleSentence: The new evidence served to exculpate the suspect entirely.

definition: To express strong disapproval or disagreement.
etymology: From Latin expostulatus, past participle of expostulare 'to demand earnestly,' from ex- plus postulare 'to demand.'
exampleSentence: She expostulated with the manager about the unfair scheduling.

definition: To make something bad or unsatisfactory better.
etymology: From French ameliorer 'to make better,' alteration of Old French ameillorer, from a- plus meillor 'better.'
exampleSentence: A short walk can ameliorate even the worst afternoon slump.

definition: To deliberately make something unclear or hard to understand.
etymology: From Latin obfuscatus, past participle of obfuscare 'to darken,' from ob- plus fuscus 'dark.'
exampleSentence: Politicians often obfuscate when a simple answer would be embarrassing.

definition: To blame or insult in strong, abusive language.
etymology: From Latin vituperatus, past participle of vituperare 'to censure,' from vitium 'fault' plus parare 'to prepare.'
exampleSentence: He vituperated the umpire until the manager dragged him off the field.

definition: Using very few words.
etymology: From Greek Lakonikos, referring to Laconia and the Spartans, who were famed for terse speech.
exampleSentence: Her laconic 'we'll see' was somehow more terrifying than a long lecture.

definition: Excessively talkative, especially about trivial things.
etymology: From Latin garrulus 'talkative,' from garrire 'to chatter.'
exampleSentence: The garrulous cab driver narrated every block of the ride.

definition: Reserved and uncommunicative in speech.
etymology: From Latin taciturnus, from tacitus 'silent,' from tacere 'to be silent.'
exampleSentence: Her taciturn uncle ate Thanksgiving dinner without saying a word.

definition: Talkative; given to chattering.
etymology: From Latin loquax 'talkative,' from loqui 'to speak.'
exampleSentence: Two glasses of wine in, our loquacious host had told us every family secret.

definition: Showing great knowledge or learning.
etymology: From Latin eruditus 'instructed,' past participle of erudire 'to polish, instruct,' from e- plus rudis 'rude, untaught.'
exampleSentence: His erudite footnotes were sometimes longer than the chapters themselves.

definition: Overly concerned with minor details or rules.
etymology: From Italian pedante 'teacher,' possibly via Vulgar Latin from Greek paideuein 'to teach.'
exampleSentence: Spare me your pedantic distinctions; I just want to know if the cake is good.

definition: Idealistic and impractical to an extreme degree.
etymology: From Don Quixote, the deluded knight in Cervantes' 1605 novel.
exampleSentence: Her quixotic plan to bicycle across the continent ended at the first hill.

definition: Cunning and unscrupulous, especially in politics.
etymology: After Niccolo Machiavelli, the sixteenth-century Florentine author of The Prince.
exampleSentence: His Machiavellian maneuvering at the board meeting impressed even his rivals.

definition: Excessively harsh and severe.
etymology: From Draco, the seventh-century BCE Athenian legislator known for his strict legal code.
exampleSentence: The new noise ordinance felt draconian to anyone who liked a backyard barbecue.

definition: Peaceful, idyllic, especially in retrospect.
etymology: From Greek alkyon 'kingfisher,' tied to a myth that the bird calmed the seas at the winter solstice.
exampleSentence: They reminisced about the halcyon summers before the move.

definition: Tending to or able to change frequently or easily.
etymology: After Proteus, the shape-shifting sea god in Greek mythology.
exampleSentence: Her protean acting career ranged from Shakespeare to slapstick comedy.

definition: Endlessly laborious and futile.
etymology: After Sisyphus, the figure in Greek myth condemned to roll a boulder uphill forever.
exampleSentence: Cleaning a toddler's room is a sisyphean task.

definition: Enduring pain or hardship without showing feelings.
etymology: From Greek Stoikos, referring to the philosophers who taught at the Stoa Poikile in Athens.
exampleSentence: He was stoic about losing the championship, though it clearly hurt.

definition: Excessive pride or self-confidence leading to a downfall.
etymology: From Greek hybris 'insolence, outrage,' originally describing violent disrespect toward gods or people.
exampleSentence: His hubris finally caught up with him during the live televised debate.

definition: The release of pent-up emotion, often through art.
etymology: From Greek katharsis 'cleansing,' from kathairein 'to purify,' used by Aristotle in his Poetics.
exampleSentence: A good cry over a sad movie can be a small catharsis.

definition: Dominance of one group over others.
etymology: From Greek hegemonia 'leadership,' from hegemon 'leader.'
exampleSentence: For decades the studio's hegemony over animation went unchallenged.

definition: The defining mood or spirit of a particular era.
etymology: From German Zeit 'time' plus Geist 'spirit,' popularized by nineteenth-century German philosophers.
exampleSentence: That sitcom somehow captured the zeitgeist of the early 2000s perfectly.

definition: Pleasure derived from another's misfortune.
etymology: From German Schaden 'harm' plus Freude 'joy,' attested in English since the nineteenth century.
exampleSentence: She felt a flicker of schadenfreude when her smug coworker spilled his coffee.

definition: A particular philosophy or worldview.
etymology: From German Welt 'world' plus Anschauung 'view,' coined by Kant in the late eighteenth century.
exampleSentence: His grandmother's weltanschauung was shaped by surviving two wars.

definition: A novel about a protagonist's psychological and moral growth.
etymology: From German Bildung 'formation, education' plus Roman 'novel,' coined by philologist Karl Morgenstern in 1819.
exampleSentence: Every other prestige TV show seems to be a bildungsroman with better lighting.

definition: A look-alike of another person.
etymology: From German Doppelganger, literally 'double-goer,' coined by novelist Jean Paul in 1796.
exampleSentence: I saw your doppelganger at the airport this morning and almost called out.

definition: An organized whole that is more than the sum of its parts.
etymology: From German Gestalt 'form, shape,' used by early-twentieth-century psychologists.
exampleSentence: The whole album has a gestalt that the singles can't quite convey.

definition: A deep anxiety, often existential.
etymology: From German Angst 'fear, anxiety,' brought into English through Kierkegaard and Freud.
exampleSentence: His teenage angst eventually crystallized into a very long novel.

definition: Evoking a keen sense of sadness or regret.
etymology: From Old French poignant 'pricking,' present participle of poindre, from Latin pungere 'to prick.'
exampleSentence: The reunion was made more poignant by the empty chair at the table.

definition: A deep, persistent sadness.
etymology: From Greek melankholia 'black bile,' from melas 'black' plus khole 'bile,' the humor once blamed for depression.
exampleSentence: A quiet melancholy settled on him whenever it rained on Sundays.

definition: Bubbly, vivacious, and full of energy.
etymology: From Latin effervescens, present participle of effervescere 'to boil up,' from ex- plus fervere 'to boil.'
exampleSentence: Her effervescent personality made the party feel twice as crowded.

definition: Cheerful and full of energy.
etymology: From Latin ebulliens, present participle of ebullire 'to bubble out,' from ex- plus bullire 'to boil.'
exampleSentence: He returned from his honeymoon ebullient and slightly sunburned.

definition: Gloomy and grave in temperament.
etymology: From Late Latin saturninus 'of Saturn,' the planet astrologically linked to a sluggish, dark mood.
exampleSentence: His saturnine expression made even job interviews feel like funerals.

definition: Subject to rapid and unpredictable changes of mood.
etymology: From Latin mercurialis 'of Mercury,' from the planet and the swift, changeable god of the same name.
exampleSentence: Her mercurial boss was hard to predict before noon.

definition: Cheerful and friendly.
etymology: From Late Latin jovialis 'of Jupiter,' the planet thought to bring a happy disposition.
exampleSentence: The jovial bartender remembered everyone's name and drink order.

definition: Relating to war or warriors.
etymology: From Latin martialis 'of Mars,' the god of war.
exampleSentence: The parade had a brisk martial cadence that woke up the entire block.

definition: Demonstrating aggression and willingness to fight.
etymology: From Latin bellicosus, from bellicus 'of war,' from bellum 'war.'
exampleSentence: His bellicose tweets did him no favors during the negotiation.

definition: Eager or quick to argue, quarrel, or fight.
etymology: From Latin pugnax 'combative,' from pugnare 'to fight,' from pugnus 'fist.'
exampleSentence: He has a pugnacious streak that helps him in court but not at dinner parties.

definition: To make someone less angry or hostile.
etymology: From Latin placatus, past participle of placare 'to calm.'
exampleSentence: She tried to placate the upset customer with a free dessert.

definition: To win or regain the favor of an offended party.
etymology: From Latin propitiatus, past participle of propitiare 'to render favorable.'
exampleSentence: He brought flowers to propitiate his furious roommate.

definition: To soothe or appease someone's anger.
etymology: From Latin mollificare 'to soften,' from mollis 'soft' plus facere 'to make.'
exampleSentence: A sincere apology might mollify her, but a half-hearted one will make things worse.

definition: To make a feeling less intense or to satisfy a need.
etymology: From Old French assouagier 'to soften,' from Latin ad- plus suavis 'sweet.'
exampleSentence: Nothing seemed to assuage her guilt about missing the recital.

definition: To become less intense or widespread.
etymology: From Old French abatre 'to beat down,' from Latin battuere 'to beat.'
exampleSentence: They waited under an awning for the storm to abate.

definition: To cease resisting; to surrender.
etymology: From Medieval Latin capitulatus, past participle of capitulare 'to draw up under headings,' from caput 'head.'
exampleSentence: After hours of debate, the union refused to capitulate on overtime pay.

definition: To formally repeal or do away with.
etymology: From Latin abrogatus, past participle of abrogare 'to repeal,' from ab- plus rogare 'to propose a law.'
exampleSentence: The new administration moved quickly to abrogate the unpopular treaty.

definition: To make widely known, especially a law or doctrine.
etymology: From Latin promulgatus, past participle of promulgare 'to make public,' related to mulgere 'to milk forth.'
exampleSentence: The agency promulgated new rules for drone flights over cities.

definition: To outline faintly or to foreshadow.
etymology: From Latin adumbratus, past participle of adumbrare 'to shadow,' from ad- plus umbra 'shadow.'
exampleSentence: The opening chapter adumbrates the tragedy that ends the novel.

definition: To solemnly renounce a belief, cause, or claim.
etymology: From Latin abjurare 'to deny on oath,' from ab- plus jurare 'to swear.'
exampleSentence: He publicly abjured the conspiracy theories he had once championed.

definition: To urge or request earnestly, often under oath.
etymology: From Latin adjurare 'to swear to,' from ad- plus jurare 'to swear.'
exampleSentence: The judge adjured the jury to weigh the evidence carefully.

definition: To speak or write about something with great hostility.
etymology: From Latin invehi 'to attack with words,' passive of invehere 'to carry against.'
exampleSentence: He inveighed against the new parking fees for nearly an hour.

definition: To persuade someone by deception or flattery.
etymology: From Anglo-French enveogler, from Old French aveugler 'to blind,' from aveugle 'blind.'
exampleSentence: She inveigled her way into the after-party without an invitation.

definition: To call into question someone's honesty or integrity.
etymology: From Latin impugnare 'to fight against,' from in- plus pugnare 'to fight.'
exampleSentence: He resented anyone who impugned his motives for volunteering.

definition: A false and malicious statement intended to damage a reputation.
etymology: From Latin calumnia 'slander,' related to calvi 'to trick.'
exampleSentence: The campaign devolved into a contest of calumny rather than ideas.

definition: An attack on someone's reputation or integrity.
etymology: From Latin aspersio 'sprinkling,' from aspergere 'to sprinkle,' originally a literal religious sprinkling.
exampleSentence: Don't cast aspersions on his work ethic without knowing his schedule.

definition: Harsh public criticism or scorn.
etymology: From Latin opprobrium 'reproach,' from ob- plus probrum 'disgraceful act.'
exampleSentence: The plagiarism scandal brought him years of opprobrium from his peers.

definition: Strong, widespread public condemnation.
etymology: From Late Latin obloquium 'contradiction,' from obloqui 'to speak against,' from ob- plus loqui 'to speak.'
exampleSentence: He endured years of obloquy before his theories were finally vindicated.

definition: Approval or praise.
etymology: From Latin approbatio, from approbare 'to approve,' from ad- plus probare 'to test, prove.'
exampleSentence: She glowed under the approbation of her notoriously stingy editor.

definition: A speech or piece of writing that praises someone or something highly.
etymology: From Greek enkomion, originally a song of praise sung at a victory procession, from en- plus komos 'revel.'
exampleSentence: His retirement party turned into a three-hour encomium.

definition: A public speech or text in praise of someone.
etymology: From Greek panegyrikos 'fit for a public assembly,' from pan 'all' plus agora 'assembly.'
exampleSentence: The introduction was less a biography than a breathless panegyric.

definition: A gesture of respect or submission.
etymology: From Old French obeissance 'obedience,' from obeir 'to obey,' from Latin oboedire.
exampleSentence: The diplomats performed careful obeisance before the new monarch.

definition: The state of feeling deep regret for wrongdoing.
etymology: From Latin contritio 'a grinding,' from conterere 'to grind,' used figuratively for crushed spirits.
exampleSentence: His apology had the quiet weight of real contrition.

definition: Feeling or showing sorrow for sin or wrongdoing.
etymology: From Latin paenitens 'regretting,' present participle of paenitere 'to cause to repent.'
exampleSentence: He looked penitent enough that she almost forgave him on the spot.

definition: Sharp and biting, especially in speech.
etymology: From Latin acerbus 'harsh, sour,' related to acer 'sharp.'
exampleSentence: His acerbic restaurant reviews could end a chef's career in a paragraph.

definition: Severely critical or sarcastic.
etymology: From Greek kaustikos 'burning,' from kaiein 'to burn.'
exampleSentence: Her caustic wit made staff meetings memorable in all the wrong ways.

definition: Vigorous, incisive, or cuttingly clear.
etymology: From Old French trenchant 'cutting,' present participle of trenchier 'to cut.'
exampleSentence: His trenchant criticism of the bill changed several senators' votes.

definition: Mocking or cynical in a grim, dry way.
etymology: From French sardonique, from Greek sardanios, linked by some ancient writers to a Sardinian plant said to cause a grim laugh.
exampleSentence: He answered the obvious question with a sardonic raise of his eyebrow.

definition: Cheerfully optimistic, especially in difficult conditions.
etymology: From Latin sanguineus 'of blood,' since the sanguine humor was thought to produce a cheerful temperament.
exampleSentence: He remained sanguine about the company's prospects even after the layoffs.

definition: Excessively ornate; or having a red, flushed complexion.
etymology: From Latin floridus 'flowery,' from flos 'flower.'
exampleSentence: His florid prose buried what could have been a moving story.

definition: Highly ornate and extravagant in style.
etymology: From Portuguese barroco 'irregular pearl,' borrowed into French to describe seventeenth-century art.
exampleSentence: The hotel's baroque lobby felt like stepping into a costume drama.

definition: Extravagantly ornate, especially in eighteenth-century French style.
etymology: From French rococo, a playful alteration of rocaille 'shellwork,' used to describe the lavish style of the era.
exampleSentence: Her wedding cake had a rococo flourish at every level.

definition: Severe or strict in manner; or having no comforts or luxuries.
etymology: From Latin austerus 'harsh, severe,' from Greek austeros 'making the tongue dry.'
exampleSentence: The monastery's austere stone cells contrasted sharply with the gilded chapel.

definition: Severely self-disciplined, avoiding pleasure and luxury.
etymology: From Greek asketikos 'practiced, athletic,' from askein 'to exercise.'
exampleSentence: Her ascetic lifestyle would impress a monk.

definition: Devoted to refined sensual pleasure, especially of food and drink.
etymology: From the Greek philosopher Epicurus, whose followers prized tranquil enjoyment of life.
exampleSentence: He took an epicurean approach to weekends and a Spartan one to weekdays.

definition: A person who pursues pleasure as the highest good.
etymology: From Greek hedone 'pleasure,' coined by ancient philosophers of the Cyrenaic school.
exampleSentence: His twenties had been a hedonist's grand tour of bad decisions.

definition: The belief that life is meaningless and that traditional values are baseless.
etymology: From Latin nihil 'nothing' plus -ism, popularized by Turgenev's novel Fathers and Sons in 1862.
exampleSentence: A streak of nihilism crept into his late paintings.

definition: The view that only the self is certain to exist.
etymology: From Latin solus 'alone' plus ipse 'self,' coined in modern Latin in the eighteenth century.
exampleSentence: His solipsism made it impossible to plan around his moods.

definition: Relating to existence, especially questions of meaning and identity.
etymology: From Latin existentia 'existence,' used in twentieth-century philosophy by Kierkegaard, Heidegger, and Sartre.
exampleSentence: A flat tire on the highway can prompt a small existential crisis.

definition: A method of argument that resolves contradictions through reasoned discussion.
etymology: From Greek dialektike 'art of discussion,' from dialegesthai 'to converse.'
exampleSentence: Their late-night debates were a dialectic of espresso and exhaustion.

definition: Clever but misleading argument.
etymology: From Greek sophistes 'wise man,' applied disparagingly by Plato to itinerant teachers who used rhetorical tricks.
exampleSentence: The TED talk dressed up old sophistry in slick animation.

definition: Clever but unsound reasoning, especially on moral questions.
etymology: From Latin casus 'case' plus -istry, originally a Jesuit approach to applying ethics to specific cases.
exampleSentence: His casuistry about tip jars revealed more than he intended.

definition: To speak or act evasively in order to avoid the truth.
etymology: From Latin praevaricatus, past participle of praevaricari 'to walk crookedly,' from prae- plus varicare 'to straddle.'
exampleSentence: Stop prevaricating and tell me whether you ate the last cookie.

definition: To use ambiguous language to conceal the truth or avoid commitment.
etymology: From Late Latin aequivocatus, past participle of aequivocare 'to call by the same name,' from aequus 'equal' plus vox 'voice.'
exampleSentence: The spokesperson equivocated until even friendly reporters lost patience.

definition: To disguise one's true feelings or motives.
etymology: From Old French dessembler 'to be unlike,' partly from Latin dissimulare 'to disguise.'
exampleSentence: He tried to dissemble his disappointment, but his face gave him away.

definition: A deceptive movement designed to mislead an opponent.
etymology: From French feinte, feminine of feint, past participle of feindre 'to feign,' from Latin fingere 'to shape.'
exampleSentence: The boxer's feint to the left set up the perfect right hook.

definition: An opening move or strategic maneuver intended to gain advantage.
etymology: From Italian gambetto 'tripping up,' originally a chess term for a pawn sacrifice.
exampleSentence: Her gambit at the start of negotiations caught the other side off guard.

definition: A crafty scheme or plot.
etymology: From Latin machinatio 'contrivance,' from machinari 'to contrive,' from machina 'device.'
exampleSentence: The boardroom was thick with machinations against the new director.

definition: The use of trickery to achieve a political, financial, or legal purpose.
etymology: From French chicanerie 'sharp practice,' from chicaner 'to quibble,' of uncertain origin.
exampleSentence: His legal team specialized in procedural chicanery.

definition: Deceit used to achieve one's goal.
etymology: From Late Latin subterfugium, from Latin subterfugere 'to escape secretly,' from subter- plus fugere 'to flee.'
exampleSentence: They reached the surprise party through a series of subterfuges and detours.

definition: Deceitfulness, especially involving double-dealing.
etymology: From Late Latin duplicitas 'doubleness,' from duplex 'twofold.'
exampleSentence: Her duplicity finally surfaced when the two stories she told didn't match.

definition: Deceitfulness; untrustworthiness.
etymology: From Latin perfidia 'faithlessness,' from per- plus fides 'faith.'
exampleSentence: He never recovered from his friend's perfidy.

definition: Depravity; wicked behavior.
etymology: From Latin turpitudo 'ugliness, baseness,' from turpis 'shameful.'
exampleSentence: The contract had a clause about moral turpitude that no one expected to invoke.

definition: Susceptible to bribery; willing to behave corruptly for money.
etymology: From Latin venalis 'for sale,' from venum 'sale.'
exampleSentence: A few venal officials had reportedly waved the shipments through.

definition: A minor sin or fault; pardonable.
etymology: From Late Latin venialis 'pardonable,' from venia 'forgiveness.'
exampleSentence: Forgetting his birthday was, in her mind, only a venial offense.

definition: Greedy for wealth or gain.
etymology: From Old French avaricius, from Latin avarus 'greedy,' from avere 'to crave.'
exampleSentence: His avaricious uncle famously charged the family rent on his couch.

definition: Marked by an inordinate desire for something belonging to another.
etymology: From Old French coveitos, from Latin cupiditas 'longing,' from cupere 'to desire.'
exampleSentence: She tried not to be covetous of her neighbor's herb garden.

definition: Extremely poor, or extremely stingy.
etymology: From Medieval Latin penuriosus, from Latin penuria 'want, need.'
exampleSentence: The biography painted a vivid picture of his penurious childhood.

definition: Unwilling to spend money; extremely frugal.
etymology: From Latin parsimonia 'frugality,' from parcere 'to spare.'
exampleSentence: His parsimonious habits made every gift exchange suspenseful.

definition: More generous than is usual or necessary.
etymology: From Latin munificus 'generous,' from munus 'gift' plus facere 'to make.'
exampleSentence: A munificent donation kept the library open for another decade.

definition: Generosity in giving, especially in bestowing gifts or money.
etymology: From Old French largesse 'bounty,' from large 'generous,' from Latin largus.
exampleSentence: The team flew first class thanks to the owner's annual largesse.

definition: The desire to promote others' welfare, often through donations.
etymology: From Greek philanthropos 'loving humankind,' from philos 'loving' plus anthropos 'human.'
exampleSentence: Late in life she turned her fortune toward philanthropy and forgot most of her enemies.

definition: A person who dislikes humankind in general.
etymology: From Greek misanthropos 'hating people,' from misein 'to hate' plus anthropos 'human.'
exampleSentence: He cultivated a misanthrope's reputation but was always the first to help a neighbor.

definition: Believing in equality for all people.
etymology: From French egalitaire, from egalite 'equality,' from Latin aequalis 'equal.'
exampleSentence: Their egalitarian household had no fixed roles for cooking or cleaning.

definition: Government by the wealthy.
etymology: From Greek ploutokratia, from ploutos 'wealth' plus -kratia 'rule.'
exampleSentence: Critics called the new tax law a giveaway to the plutocracy.

definition: Government by a small group of people.
etymology: From Greek oligarkhia, from oligoi 'few' plus arkhein 'to rule.'
exampleSentence: A handful of families ran the city like a polite oligarchy.

definition: A government ruled by religious leaders.
etymology: From Greek theokratia, from theos 'god' plus -kratia 'rule.'
exampleSentence: The novel imagines a future theocracy reached by way of a long blackout.

definition: A system in which advancement is based on ability or achievement.
etymology: Coined by British sociologist Michael Young in 1958, combining Latin meritum 'merit' with Greek -kratia 'rule.'
exampleSentence: The firm advertised itself as a meritocracy, though the partners all knew each other from college.

definition: A leader who exploits popular prejudices and emotions.
etymology: From Greek demagogos 'popular leader,' from demos 'people' plus agogos 'leading.'
exampleSentence: Every era seems to find a fresh demagogue ready for the moment.

definition: A strong written or spoken attack on someone's opinions.
etymology: From Greek polemikos 'warlike,' from polemos 'war.'
exampleSentence: His op-ed was less an argument than a polemic.

definition: A long, angry speech or piece of writing.
etymology: From Greek diatribe 'discourse,' originally 'wearing away,' from dia- plus tribein 'to rub.'
exampleSentence: A simple ask about the WiFi password unleashed a diatribe about modern life.

definition: A lengthy, aggressive speech.
etymology: From Old Italian aringa 'public square speech,' from aringare 'to address an assembly.'
exampleSentence: The coach's halftime harangue could be heard in the parking lot.

definition: A long, mournful complaint or lament.
etymology: From French jeremiade, after the biblical prophet Jeremiah, traditionally credited with the Book of Lamentations.
exampleSentence: His annual holiday letter is mostly a jeremiad about the post office.

definition: A bitter denunciation.
etymology: From Greek philippikos, applied to Demosthenes's speeches against Philip II of Macedon.
exampleSentence: Her philippic against the new dress code lit up the staff chat.

definition: Insulting or abusive language.
etymology: From Late Latin invectiva 'abusive speech,' from invehi 'to attack with words.'
exampleSentence: He launched into invective the moment the camera turned off.

definition: Cruel and bitter criticism.
etymology: From Medieval Latin vitriolum 'sulfate,' originally referring to the corrosive substance, used figuratively for caustic speech.
exampleSentence: There was real vitriol in his goodbye message.

definition: Bitter, sharp-tempered behavior or speech.
etymology: From Latin acrimonia 'sharpness,' from acer 'sharp.'
exampleSentence: The divorce proceeded with surprising acrimony given how dull the marriage had been.

definition: Bitter, long-lasting ill feeling.
etymology: From Late Latin rancor 'rancidity, grudge,' related to rancere 'to stink.'
exampleSentence: After fifteen years, the rancor between the brothers had hardened into silence.

definition: Active, often mutual hostility.
etymology: From Old French enemistie, from Latin inimicitia, from inimicus 'enemy.'
exampleSentence: The longstanding enmity between the two families flared up at the school play.

definition: Hostility or ill feeling.
etymology: From Latin animus 'mind, spirit, anger,' related to anima 'breath, soul.'
exampleSentence: There was no political animus in his vote, just stubborn principle.

definition: Offense or annoyance.
etymology: From Old French ombrage 'shadow,' from Latin umbra 'shade,' developed figuratively to mean a sense of shadow cast on one's pride.
exampleSentence: She took umbrage at the suggestion that she might be tired.

definition: A feeling of offense or deep resentment.
etymology: Of obscure origin, first attested in the sixteenth century in the phrase 'in high dudgeon.'
exampleSentence: He stalked out of the meeting in high dudgeon.

definition: Anger or irritability.
etymology: From Greek khole 'bile,' the bodily humor once thought to govern irritability.
exampleSentence: A second cup of coffee did nothing to settle her morning choler.

definition: Irritable, gloomy, or peevish.
etymology: From Greek dyspepsia 'bad digestion,' from dys- plus pepsis 'digestion,' since irritability was associated with poor digestion.
exampleSentence: His dyspeptic reviews were the only reason anyone read the column.

definition: Habitually complaining.
etymology: From Latin querulus 'complaining,' from queri 'to complain.'
exampleSentence: The querulous diner sent back two appetizers before finally settling on toast.

definition: Tending to find fault or raise petty objections.
etymology: From Latin captiosus 'fallacious, deceptive,' from captio 'a trick.'
exampleSentence: His captious feedback added hours to every revision cycle.

definition: Severely critical of others.
etymology: From Latin censorius 'pertaining to a censor,' from censor, the Roman official who judged morals.
exampleSentence: The book club had grown more censorious than literary.

definition: Behaving as though one is superior to others.
etymology: From Latin superciliosus, from supercilium 'eyebrow,' from the gesture of raising the brow in disdain.
exampleSentence: A supercilious sommelier nearly ruined the date before the appetizers arrived.

definition: Arrogantly superior and disdainful.
etymology: From Old French haut 'high,' from Latin altus, with an added -gh- by analogy with English words like 'caught.'
exampleSentence: She gave him a haughty look that could have peeled paint.

definition: Assuming power or authority without justification.
etymology: From Latin imperiosus, from imperium 'authority, command.'
exampleSentence: His imperious manner made the intern visibly flinch.

definition: Insisting on immediate attention or obedience.
etymology: From Latin peremptorius 'deadly, decisive,' from perimere 'to destroy.'
exampleSentence: She issued a peremptory command and walked out before anyone could answer.

definition: Aggressively offering unwanted help or advice.
etymology: From Latin officiosus 'obliging,' from officium 'duty,' which acquired a negative connotation in English.
exampleSentence: An officious neighbor reorganized the recycling bins again.

definition: Persistent and demanding to the point of annoyance.
etymology: From Latin importunus 'troublesome,' from in- plus portus 'harbor,' originally describing weather unfit for sailing into port.
exampleSentence: She fielded importunate texts from him every hour.

definition: Casually unconcerned.
etymology: From French insouciant, from in- plus soucier 'to trouble,' from Latin sollicitare.
exampleSentence: His insouciant shrug irritated everyone in the room.

definition: Feeling or appearing calm and relaxed.
etymology: From Old French nonchaloir 'to disregard,' from non- plus chaloir 'to be concerned,' from Latin calere 'to be warm.'
exampleSentence: She gave a nonchalant wave as she boarded the plane to her new life.

definition: Unimpressed or indifferent due to overexposure.
etymology: From French blase, past participle of blaser 'to satiate.'
exampleSentence: Even the blase travel writer admitted the fjord was extraordinary.

definition: Tired, bored, or lacking enthusiasm from overexposure.
etymology: From earlier English jade 'worn-out horse,' of uncertain origin, perhaps related to a Norse word for a mare.
exampleSentence: After ten years in tech, he was thoroughly jaded by buzzwords.

definition: To accustom someone to something unpleasant.
etymology: From earlier English in ure 'in use,' from Anglo-French ure 'work, custom,' from Latin opera.
exampleSentence: Years of late shifts had inured him to the smell of stale coffee.

definition: To adjust to a new climate, environment, or situation.
etymology: From French acclimater, from a- plus climat 'climate.'
exampleSentence: Give yourself a few days to acclimate to the altitude before hiking.

definition: To leave hurriedly and secretly, usually to avoid consequences.
etymology: From Latin abscondere 'to hide,' from abs- plus condere 'to put away.'
exampleSentence: The treasurer absconded with the petty cash and a stapler.

definition: To depart suddenly, often secretly.
etymology: From French decamper, originally a military term meaning to strike camp, from de- plus camp.
exampleSentence: They decamped to the beach as soon as school let out.

definition: To renounce a throne, high office, or responsibility.
etymology: From Latin abdicatus, past participle of abdicare 'to disown,' from ab- plus dicare 'to proclaim.'
exampleSentence: He effectively abdicated his role as team lead after the third missed deadline.

definition: To go back on a promise or commitment.
etymology: From Medieval Latin renegare 'to deny,' from re- plus negare 'to deny.'
exampleSentence: The studio reneged on the offer at the last possible moment.

definition: To withdraw a previous statement or belief, often publicly.
etymology: From Latin recantare 'to sing back, retract,' from re- plus cantare 'to sing.'
exampleSentence: He refused to recant the column despite the lawsuit.

definition: To revoke or cancel officially.
etymology: From Latin rescindere 'to cut off,' from re- plus scindere 'to cut.'
exampleSentence: The university rescinded the honorary degree after the scandal broke.

definition: To renounce or reject something desired.
etymology: From Latin abnegatus, past participle of abnegare 'to refuse,' from ab- plus negare 'to deny.'
exampleSentence: She had to abnegate any claim to the inheritance before signing.

definition: To solemnly give up or renounce.
etymology: From Old English forswerian, from for- 'completely' plus swerian 'to swear.'
exampleSentence: He forswore sweets every January and broke his vow every February.

definition: To deliberately avoid or abstain from something.
etymology: From Old French eschiver 'to shun,' from Frankish skiuhan 'to dread.'
exampleSentence: Most chefs at the festival eschew shortcuts in favor of slow cooking.

definition: Sparing, especially in eating and drinking.
etymology: From Latin abstemius 'sober,' from abs- plus temetum 'intoxicating drink.'
exampleSentence: He maintained an abstemious diet of toast and weak tea.

definition: Self-restrained; moderate.
etymology: From Latin temperatus, past participle of temperare 'to mix in due proportion.'
exampleSentence: His temperate response defused what could have been an ugly argument.

definition: Spending money or resources freely and recklessly.
etymology: From Latin prodigus 'wasteful,' from prodigere 'to drive away, waste,' from pro- plus agere 'to drive.'
exampleSentence: His prodigal weekend in Vegas wiped out a year of savings.

definition: Recklessly extravagant or wasteful.
etymology: From Latin profligatus 'broken down in character,' past participle of profligare 'to strike down,' from pro- plus fligere 'to strike.'
exampleSentence: The profligate spending in his first term came back to haunt him.

definition: Unable to pay one's debts.
etymology: From Latin in- 'not' plus solvens, present participle of solvere 'to loosen, pay.'
exampleSentence: The once-mighty retailer filed insolvent in a single dramatic week.

definition: Poor; needy.
etymology: From Latin indigens, present participle of indigere 'to need,' from indu- 'in' plus egere 'to need.'
exampleSentence: The clinic offered free dental care to indigent residents of the county.

definition: Having little or no money.
etymology: From in- 'not' plus Latin pecuniosus 'rich,' from pecunia 'money,' from pecu 'cattle,' once a measure of wealth.
exampleSentence: He spent his impecunious twenties living off coffee and free bread.

definition: Having a great deal of money; wealthy.
etymology: From Latin affluens 'flowing toward,' from ad- plus fluere 'to flow.'
exampleSentence: The town's most affluent neighborhood elects its own mayor every other year.

definition: Ostentatiously rich and luxurious.
etymology: From Latin opulentus 'wealthy,' related to opes 'wealth, resources.'
exampleSentence: The lobby was opulent in the way only old hotels can manage.

definition: Splendid and expensive-looking.
etymology: From Latin sumptuosus 'costly,' from sumptus 'expense,' from sumere 'to take, spend.'
exampleSentence: They sat down to a sumptuous twelve-course tasting menu.

definition: Generous or extravagant.
etymology: From Old French lavache 'deluge of rain,' from laver 'to wash,' from Latin lavare.
exampleSentence: She received lavish praise from a critic who usually hated everything.

definition: Abundant or copious; given freely.
etymology: From Latin profusus 'poured forth,' past participle of profundere, from pro- plus fundere 'to pour.'
exampleSentence: He offered profuse apologies and an even more profuse bouquet.

definition: Abundant in supply or quantity.
etymology: From Latin copiosus, from copia 'plenty,' from co- plus ops 'wealth, resources.'
exampleSentence: She took copious notes during the lecture and ignored every Zoom message.

definition: Producing many works, results, or offspring.
etymology: From French prolifique, from Latin proles 'offspring' plus -ficus 'making.'
exampleSentence: The prolific cartoonist had filed a strip every weekday for forty years.

definition: Remarkably or impressively great in size, force, or extent.
etymology: From Latin prodigiosus 'marvelous,' from prodigium 'omen, marvel.'
exampleSentence: He had a prodigious memory for batting averages and birthday cards alike.

definition: Extremely large or great.
etymology: From Latin colossus, from Greek kolossos, originally a huge statue, famously the Colossus of Rhodes.
exampleSentence: The colossal sculpture in the lobby seemed to lean over visitors.

definition: A huge or monstrous creature or thing.
etymology: From Hebrew behemot, a plural of intensification of behemah 'beast,' referring to a creature in the Book of Job.
exampleSentence: The new aircraft carrier is a behemoth that dwarfs the destroyers beside it.

definition: A very large or powerful thing, especially of the sea or in government.
etymology: From Hebrew livyathan, a sea monster in the Hebrew Bible, used by Hobbes for the state.
exampleSentence: Bureaucracy can become a leviathan that no minister truly controls.

definition: A massive, overwhelming force or institution.
etymology: From Hindi Jagannath 'lord of the world,' a title of Krishna, after the heavy chariot used in his processions.
exampleSentence: The streaming juggernaut absorbed yet another smaller studio.

definition: A person or thing of enormous size, power, or influence.
etymology: From Greek kolossos, a huge statue, especially the Colossus of Rhodes.
exampleSentence: For decades he was the colossus of investigative journalism.

definition: Of exceptional strength, size, or power.
etymology: From Greek Titanikos, after the Titans, the elder gods overthrown by the Olympians.
exampleSentence: They were locked in a titanic struggle over a parking space.

definition: Extremely small.
etymology: From modern Latin infinitesimus 'the n-th term in an infinite series,' from infinitus 'infinite.'
exampleSentence: The difference between the two recordings is infinitesimal.

definition: Extremely or unusually small.
etymology: From Latin diminutivus, from diminuere 'to lessen.'
exampleSentence: The diminutive coach somehow filled the entire sideline.

definition: Extremely small; tiny.
etymology: From Latin minuscula littera 'small letter,' feminine of minusculus, diminutive of minor 'less.'
exampleSentence: A minuscule chip in the lens turned the photo into an abstract painting.

definition: So small or unimportant as not to be worth considering.
etymology: From Latin neglegere 'to neglect,' from neg- 'not' plus legere 'to pick up, choose.'
exampleSentence: The fee for international transfers was once negligible; not anymore.

definition: Of little value or importance.
etymology: From Latin trivialis 'commonplace,' from trivium 'three roads,' a crossroads where common gossip was exchanged.
exampleSentence: What seems trivial today often becomes important by Friday.

definition: So lacking in originality as to be obvious and boring.
etymology: From French banal 'common,' originally 'pertaining to compulsory feudal service.'
exampleSentence: His speech alternated between banal advice and genuinely strange anecdotes.

definition: Lacking originality through overuse.
etymology: From English hackney 'a horse let out for hire,' from Hackney, a London district once known for breeding such horses.
exampleSentence: The script leaned on hackneyed jokes about airline food.

definition: Overused and consequently of little impact.
etymology: From Latin tritus 'worn,' past participle of terere 'to rub.'
exampleSentence: Avoid trite metaphors about journeys and storms in your wedding toast.

definition: Offering nothing that is stimulating or challenging.
etymology: From Latin vapidus 'flat, insipid,' related to vappa 'flat wine.'
exampleSentence: The interview produced one vapid quote after another.

definition: Lacking flavor, vigor, or interest.
etymology: From Late Latin insipidus, from in- 'not' plus sapidus 'tasty,' from sapere 'to taste.'
exampleSentence: The dressing made an otherwise sharp salad taste insipid.

definition: Having the dullness of prose; commonplace.
etymology: From Late Latin prosaicus 'in prose,' from prosa 'prose,' as contrasted with poetry.
exampleSentence: The truth turned out to be prosaic: he had simply forgotten the keys.

definition: Of or occurring every day; ordinary.
etymology: From Latin quotidianus, from quotidie 'daily,' from quot 'how many' plus dies 'day.'
exampleSentence: The novel finds quiet drama in the most quotidian moments.

definition: Lacking inspiration or excitement; dull.
etymology: From Latin pedester 'going on foot,' from pes 'foot,' applied figuratively to plain or dull style.
exampleSentence: His criticism was that the film was technically polished but emotionally pedestrian.

definition: Lacking interest or excitement; dull.
etymology: From Latin mundanus 'of the world,' from mundus 'world.'
exampleSentence: After the trip everything felt mundane, even her favorite coffee shop.

definition: Routine and mechanical; unimaginative.
etymology: From Greek banausikos 'pertaining to artisans,' from banausos 'manual laborer,' a term Aristotle used dismissively.
exampleSentence: He found the banausic side of academic life harder to bear than the politics.

definition: Carried out with minimum effort or care.
etymology: From Late Latin perfunctorius 'careless,' from perfunctus, past participle of perfungi 'to perform, get through.'
exampleSentence: His perfunctory thanks barely qualified as gratitude.

definition: Hasty and not thorough.
etymology: From Latin cursorius 'pertaining to running,' from cursor 'runner,' from currere 'to run.'
exampleSentence: A cursory glance at the contract missed the very expensive footnote.

definition: Showing great attention to detail.
etymology: From Latin meticulosus 'fearful,' from metus 'fear,' shifting in meaning toward overly careful.
exampleSentence: His meticulous record-keeping made the audit almost pleasant.

definition: Diligent, thorough, and extremely attentive to details.
etymology: From Latin scrupulosus, from scrupus 'sharp stone,' a small worry like a pebble in the shoe.
exampleSentence: She was scrupulous about citing every source, even the obvious ones.

definition: Showing great attention to detail or correct behavior.
etymology: From Italian puntiglioso, from puntiglio 'point of honor,' from Latin punctum 'a point.'
exampleSentence: He was punctilious about returning library books on the actual due date.

definition: Showing great care, attention, and effort.
etymology: From Latin assiduus 'persistent,' from assidere 'to sit beside,' from ad- plus sedere 'to sit.'
exampleSentence: Her assiduous research turned up letters no historian had ever cited.

definition: Showing dedication and diligence.
etymology: From Latin sedulus 'attentive, zealous,' from sedulo 'sincerely,' from se- 'without' plus dolus 'guile.'
exampleSentence: Sedulous practice turned an awkward beginner into a regional champion.

definition: Persisting tirelessly.
etymology: From Latin indefatigabilis, from in- 'not' plus defatigare 'to tire out.'
exampleSentence: The indefatigable volunteers staffed the hotline through the night.

definition: Fearless; adventurous.
etymology: From Latin intrepidus, from in- 'not' plus trepidus 'alarmed.'
exampleSentence: An intrepid reporter waded into the flooded basement to find the source.

definition: Showing fearlessness and determination.
etymology: From English daunt, from Old French danter, from Latin domitare 'to tame.'
exampleSentence: The dauntless hiker pressed on despite the worsening weather.

definition: Possessing or showing courage.
etymology: From Old French vaillant 'worthy, brave,' present participle of valoir 'to be worth,' from Latin valere 'to be strong.'
exampleSentence: It was a valiant effort, but the souffle still collapsed.

definition: Formidable, especially as an opponent; commanding respect.
etymology: From Old French redoutable, from redouter 'to dread,' from re- plus douter 'to fear.'
exampleSentence: His redoubtable serve made him a finalist year after year.

definition: Inspiring fear or respect through being impressively powerful.
etymology: From Latin formidabilis, from formidare 'to fear,' from formido 'fear.'
exampleSentence: She built a formidable reputation in the courtroom in less than a decade.

definition: Impossible to subdue or defeat.
etymology: From Late Latin indomitabilis, from in- 'not' plus domitare 'to tame.'
exampleSentence: His indomitable optimism was both his strength and his blind spot.

definition: Admirably purposeful and determined.
etymology: From Latin resolutus, past participle of resolvere 'to loosen, settle,' from re- plus solvere 'to loosen.'
exampleSentence: She remained resolute in the face of three increasingly tempting counteroffers.

definition: Tireless; persistent.
etymology: From English un- plus flag 'to droop, become weak,' of obscure origin.
exampleSentence: Her unflagging support kept the project alive through three administrations.

definition: Loyal, reliable, and hardworking.
etymology: From Old English staelwierthe 'serviceable,' probably from stathol 'foundation' plus wierthe 'worth.'
exampleSentence: A few stalwart fans stayed in the rain until the encore.

definition: Firm in purpose or belief.
etymology: From Old English stedefaest, from stede 'place' plus faest 'fixed.'
exampleSentence: He was steadfast in his refusal to read reviews of his own work.

definition: Refusing to be persuaded or to change one's mind.
etymology: From Greek adamas 'invincible,' originally a legendary unbreakable stone, often identified with diamond.
exampleSentence: He was adamant that the dog stay off the new couch.

definition: Unwilling or refusing to change one's views or to agree.
etymology: From Spanish intransigente, from in- plus transigir 'to compromise,' from Latin transigere.
exampleSentence: Both sides were intransigent, so the talks went nowhere for months.

definition: Stubbornly disobedient to authority.
etymology: From Latin contumax 'haughty, stubborn,' possibly from con- plus tumere 'to swell.'
exampleSentence: The judge found the witness contumacious and fined her on the spot.

definition: Stubborn or unmanageable.
etymology: From Latin refractarius 'obstinate,' from refringere 'to break up,' from re- plus frangere 'to break.'
exampleSentence: A refractory mule blocked the only narrow trail for an hour.

definition: Stubbornly refusing to change one's opinion or course.
etymology: From Latin obstinatus 'resolute,' past participle of obstinare 'to persist,' from ob- plus stare 'to stand.'
exampleSentence: Her obstinate refusal to use spreadsheets eventually cost her a promotion.

definition: Stubborn and unyielding.
etymology: From English mule, the famously obstinate offspring of a donkey and horse, ultimately from Latin mulus.
exampleSentence: His mulish insistence on driving turned a three-hour trip into seven.

definition: Holding firmly to an opinion or course of action.
etymology: From Latin pertinax 'holding fast,' from per- plus tenax 'tenacious.'
exampleSentence: A pertinacious researcher will eventually find the missing footnote.

definition: Holding fast; not easily dispelled or removed.
etymology: From Latin tenax 'holding fast,' from tenere 'to hold.'
exampleSentence: The cat was tenacious enough to scale the bookshelf for the dangling string.

definition: Showing tenacity or grim persistence.
etymology: From English dog plus -ed, evoking a dog's persistent grip.
exampleSentence: Her dogged pursuit of records uncovered a forgotten Olympic champion.

definition: Firm determination to do something.
etymology: From Latin resolvere 'to loosen, decide,' from re- plus solvere 'to loosen.'
exampleSentence: Her resolve hardened the moment they told her it couldn't be done.

definition: Strength of mind in adversity.
etymology: From Latin fortitudo 'strength,' from fortis 'strong.'
exampleSentence: Recovering from the injury required as much fortitude as training had.

definition: A person's ability to cope well with difficulties.
etymology: A variant spelling of metal, used figuratively in the sixteenth century to mean character or temper.
exampleSentence: The freshman quarterback showed his mettle in the season opener.

definition: Spirited and determined courage.
etymology: From English pluck 'to pull,' originally referring to a butcher's term for the heart, liver, and lungs.
exampleSentence: It took serious pluck to challenge the manager in front of his boss.

definition: Refusal to change one's views or agree to compromise.
etymology: From Spanish intransigente, used originally of an uncompromising political faction in the 1870s.
exampleSentence: Their intransigence on remote work cost them several talented hires.

definition: The quality of being shrewd and discerning.
etymology: From Latin sagacitas, from sagax 'keen,' related to sagire 'to perceive keenly.'
exampleSentence: His sagacity in business was matched only by his terrible taste in shirts.

definition: The ability to make good judgments quickly.
etymology: From Latin acumen 'sharpness,' from acuere 'to sharpen,' from acus 'needle.'
exampleSentence: Her business acumen turned a small bookstore into a small empire.

definition: Clearness and lucidity of expression.
etymology: From Latin perspicuitas, from perspicere 'to look through.'
exampleSentence: The judge praised the brief's perspicuity in an otherwise tangled case.

definition: Clarity of thought or style.
etymology: From Latin lucidus 'bright, clear,' from lux 'light.'
exampleSentence: In his final years he had moments of remarkable lucidity at dawn.

definition: The supposed ability to perceive events beyond normal sensory contact.
etymology: From French clairvoyance, from clair 'clear' plus voyant 'seeing,' from Latin clarus and videre.
exampleSentence: His investing track record looked like clairvoyance, though he just read more carefully.

definition: The fact of knowing something in advance; foresight.
etymology: From Latin praescientia, from praesciens 'knowing beforehand,' from prae- plus scire 'to know.'
exampleSentence: The novel's prescience about social media unsettled readers a decade later.

definition: The supposed ability to hear sounds beyond normal range.
etymology: From French clair 'clear' plus Latin audientia 'hearing,' from audire 'to hear.'
exampleSentence: The medium claimed clairaudience in three languages, none of them living.

definition: The practice of seeking knowledge of the future by supernatural means.
etymology: From Latin divinatio 'foreseeing,' from divinus 'divine.'
exampleSentence: Roman priests practiced divination by reading the entrails of sacrificed animals.

definition: A sign or omen; the practice of interpreting omens.
etymology: From Latin augurium 'omen,' from augur, a Roman priest who interpreted bird flight.
exampleSentence: The early rain was a poor augury for an outdoor wedding.

definition: A sign that something momentous is about to happen.
etymology: From Latin portentum 'omen,' from portendere 'to foretell,' from por- plus tendere 'to stretch.'
exampleSentence: The sudden silence in the boardroom felt like a portent of bad news.

definition: A person or thing that announces or signals something to come.
etymology: From Old French herbergere 'host, one who provides lodging,' later applied to a herald who arranged lodging for an arriving party.
exampleSentence: The first crocus is a reliable harbinger of spring.

definition: To be a sign or warning of something to come.
etymology: From Latin praesagire 'to forebode,' from prae- plus sagire 'to perceive keenly.'
exampleSentence: Quiet trading floors can presage a market downturn.

definition: To indicate a future event in advance.
etymology: From English fore- 'in front of' plus shadow, used figuratively since the sixteenth century.
exampleSentence: The opening scene quietly foreshadows the entire tragedy.

definition: To be a warning of something bad to come.
etymology: From English fore- plus bode 'to announce in advance,' from Old English bodian.
exampleSentence: A dropping barometer foreboded a rough night on the boat.

definition: To foretell or prophesy based on signs or symptoms.
etymology: From Medieval Latin prognosticatus, from prognosticum 'sign,' from Greek prognostikon, from progignoskein 'to know in advance.'
exampleSentence: Analysts love to prognosticate every January and revise every July.

definition: To be a sign of a likely outcome.
etymology: From Latin augurari 'to predict,' from augur, the Roman priest of bird signs.
exampleSentence: Her enthusiastic first day at the firm augured well for the rest of the summer.

definition: Indicating a good chance of success; favorable.
etymology: From Latin propitius 'favorable,' originally a religious term for gods being well-disposed.
exampleSentence: A clear sky and a tailwind made for a propitious start to the marathon.

definition: Giving or suggesting a sign of future success.
etymology: From Latin auspicium 'observation of birds,' from auspex 'bird-watcher,' from avis 'bird' plus specere 'to look.'
exampleSentence: His auspicious debut album made every subsequent release feel measured.

definition: Not conducive to success; unpromising.
etymology: From in- 'not' plus Latin auspicium 'omen,' from auspex 'bird-watcher.'
exampleSentence: It was an inauspicious morning that began with two flat tires.

definition: Unexpected and inappropriate or inconvenient.
etymology: From English un- plus toward 'docile,' from Old English toweard.
exampleSentence: Nothing untoward happened during the inspection, much to everyone's relief.

definition: Not able to be maintained or defended against attack or objection.
etymology: From un- plus tenable, from French tenir 'to hold,' from Latin tenere.
exampleSentence: His position became untenable once the emails surfaced.

definition: Able to be defended against attack or objection.
etymology: From French tenable, from tenir 'to hold,' from Latin tenere.
exampleSentence: The argument is tenable, even if it isn't ultimately convincing.

definition: Seeming reasonable but actually wrong.
etymology: From Latin speciosus 'beautiful, plausible,' from species 'appearance,' from specere 'to look.'
exampleSentence: His specious reasoning about overtime didn't hold up for ten seconds.

definition: Not what it purports to be; false or fake.
etymology: From Latin spurius 'false, illegitimate,' of uncertain origin.
exampleSentence: The auction catalog flagged the painting as spurious only in the fine print.

definition: Hoped for but illusory or impossible to achieve.
etymology: From Chimera, the Greek mythological monster combining lion, goat, and serpent.
exampleSentence: His chimerical scheme to colonize the Moon by Tuesday raised concerns.

definition: Based on illusion; not real.
etymology: From Late Latin illusorius, from Latin illudere 'to mock,' from in- plus ludere 'to play.'
exampleSentence: Her sense of safety on the empty street proved illusory.

definition: Apparent or stated, but not necessarily true.
etymology: From Latin ostensibilis, from ostendere 'to show,' from ob- plus tendere 'to stretch.'
exampleSentence: The ostensible reason for the meeting was a budget review.

definition: Kept secret because it would not be approved of.
etymology: From Latin surrepticius 'stolen, secret,' from surripere 'to take secretly,' from sub- plus rapere 'to seize.'
exampleSentence: He took a surreptitious photo of the whiteboard before anyone noticed.

definition: Kept secret, especially because illicit.
etymology: From Latin clandestinus, from clam 'secretly.'
exampleSentence: Their clandestine meetings at the diner became part of newsroom legend.

definition: Not openly acknowledged or displayed.
etymology: From Old French covert 'covered,' past participle of covrir 'to cover,' from Latin cooperire.
exampleSentence: There was a covert glance between them that everyone noticed.

definition: Attempting to avoid notice or attention.
etymology: From Latin furtivus 'stolen, secret,' from fur 'thief.'
exampleSentence: She made a furtive grab for the last cookie before anyone could object.

definition: Difficult to understand.
etymology: From Latin abstrusus 'hidden away,' past participle of abstrudere 'to push away,' from abs- plus trudere 'to thrust.'
exampleSentence: His abstruse theorems took whole pages to define a single symbol.

definition: Understood by few; mysterious.
etymology: From Latin arcanus 'secret,' from arcere 'to shut in,' from arca 'chest, box.'
exampleSentence: The arcane tax form had a question about gold mining I could not answer.

definition: Intended for or understood by only a small group with special knowledge.
etymology: From Greek esoterikos 'inner, belonging to an inner circle,' from eso 'within.'
exampleSentence: He had an esoteric hobby restoring vintage music boxes.

definition: Sealed off from outside influence; airtight.
etymology: From Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary alchemist credited with inventing an airtight seal.
exampleSentence: The lab kept the samples in hermetic containers for three decades.

definition: Not allowing entrance or passage; impenetrable.
etymology: From Latin impervius, from in- plus pervius 'penetrable,' from per- plus via 'way.'
exampleSentence: He seemed impervious to criticism of his cooking.

definition: Unable to be captured or broken into.
etymology: From Old French imprenable, from in- plus prendre 'to take,' from Latin prendere.
exampleSentence: The fortress was thought impregnable until a goat path was discovered.

definition: Never to be broken, infringed, or dishonored.
etymology: From Latin inviolabilis, from in- plus violare 'to violate.'
exampleSentence: Sunday breakfast in that house was inviolable.

definition: Regarded as too important or valuable to be interfered with.
etymology: From Latin sacrosanctus, from sacer 'sacred' plus sanctus 'holy.'
exampleSentence: His nap time was sacrosanct, even to the dog.

definition: Equivalent in seriousness to.
etymology: From Anglo-French tant amunter 'to amount to as much,' from Latin tantum 'so much' plus amount.
exampleSentence: Refusing to testify was tantamount to admitting guilt in the public eye.

definition: An excessive amount of something.
etymology: From Old French surfait 'overdone,' past participle of surfaire 'to overdo,' from sur- plus faire 'to do.'
exampleSentence: A surfeit of cheese at the wedding led to some unexpected naps.

definition: A large or excessive amount of something.
etymology: From Greek plethore 'fullness,' from plethein 'to be full,' originally a medical term for too much blood.
exampleSentence: There was a plethora of streaming options and nothing to watch.

definition: An excessive supply.
etymology: From Middle English glutten 'to feed gluttonously,' related to Latin gluttire 'to swallow.'
exampleSentence: A glut of avocados crashed local prices for a single strange month.

definition: A scarcity or lack of something.
etymology: From Middle English derthe 'costliness,' from dere 'dear, costly,' from Old English deore.
exampleSentence: There was a dearth of cabs at the airport at four in the morning.

definition: A small or insufficient amount.
etymology: From Latin paucitas, from paucus 'few.'
exampleSentence: The paucity of evidence forced the prosecutor to drop the charges.

definition: A very large quantity of something.
etymology: From Latin abundantia, from abundare 'to overflow,' from ab- plus unda 'wave.'
exampleSentence: There was an abundance of opinions and a shortage of decisions.

definition: A symbol of plenty; an abundant supply.
etymology: From Latin cornu copiae 'horn of plenty,' from a mythological goat's horn that overflowed with food.
exampleSentence: The farmer's market was a cornucopia of late-summer tomatoes.

definition: Generosity; an abundant supply.
etymology: From Old French bonte 'goodness,' from Latin bonitas, from bonus 'good.'
exampleSentence: They feasted on the bounty of the garden well into October.

definition: Unnecessary, especially through being more than enough.
etymology: From Latin superfluus 'overflowing,' from super- plus fluere 'to flow.'
exampleSentence: His three exclamation marks felt superfluous, but he sent the email anyway.

definition: Not or no longer needed or useful; superfluous.
etymology: From Latin redundans, present participle of redundare 'to overflow,' from red- plus undare 'to surge.'
exampleSentence: Two sentences saying the same thing make the paragraph redundant.

definition: Irrelevant or unrelated to the subject being dealt with.
etymology: From Latin extraneus 'external,' from extra 'outside.'
exampleSentence: She trimmed every extraneous adjective until the chapter sang.

definition: Relevant or applicable to a particular matter.
etymology: From Latin pertinens, present participle of pertinere 'to relate to,' from per- plus tenere 'to hold.'
exampleSentence: He asked a pertinent question that reframed the entire debate.

definition: Relevant to a subject under consideration.
etymology: From Middle English germain 'closely related,' from Old French germain, from Latin germanus 'of the same parents.'
exampleSentence: His childhood stories were touching but not germane to the budget meeting.

definition: Apt in the circumstances; very appropriate.
etymology: From Latin appositus, past participle of apponere 'to put near,' from ad- plus ponere 'to put.'
exampleSentence: Her quotation from Marcus Aurelius was strangely apposite.

definition: Well chosen or apt; pleasing.
etymology: From Latin felicitas 'happiness,' from felix 'happy.'
exampleSentence: He has a felicitous turn of phrase that makes even ordinary stories shine.

definition: Inappropriate or awkward, especially in expression.
etymology: From in- plus felicitous, from Latin felicitas 'happiness.'
exampleSentence: His infelicitous toast accidentally insulted both the bride and the caterer.

definition: Very appropriate to a particular situation.
etymology: From French a propos 'to the purpose,' from a 'to' plus propos 'purpose,' from Latin propositum.
exampleSentence: Her remark was, apropos of nothing, brutally accurate.

definition: Nearness in place or relationship.
etymology: From Latin propinquitas, from propinquus 'near,' from prope 'near.'
exampleSentence: Their propinquity at work eventually became a relationship and then a wedding.

definition: Nearness in space, time, or relationship.
etymology: From Latin proximitas, from proximus 'nearest,' superlative of prope 'near.'
exampleSentence: The rent was high mostly because of the apartment's proximity to the park.

definition: Sharing a common border; touching.
etymology: From Latin contiguus 'touching,' from contingere 'to touch on all sides.'
exampleSentence: His farm was contiguous with the national forest, which made hunting tricky.

definition: A continuous sequence in which adjacent elements are not perceptibly different.
etymology: From Latin continuum 'a continuous thing,' neuter of continuus 'continuous.'
exampleSentence: Office decor exists on a continuum from spartan to feral.

definition: To place close together for contrasting effect.
etymology: From French juxtaposer, from Latin juxta 'next to' plus French poser 'to place.'
exampleSentence: The gallery juxtaposed medieval icons with 1980s graffiti.

definition: A sharp division between two contrasting things.
etymology: From Greek dikhotomia, from dikha 'in two' plus -tomia 'cutting.'
exampleSentence: The classic dichotomy between art and commerce dissolves once rent is involved.

definition: A typical example or pattern; a framework.
etymology: From Greek paradeigma 'pattern,' from paradeiknynai 'to show side by side.'
exampleSentence: The new paradigm in publishing seems to involve TikTok at every step.

definition: A perfect example or original model.
etymology: From Greek arkhetypon, from arkhe- 'first' plus typos 'pattern.'
exampleSentence: The hard-boiled detective is the archetype of the noir hero.

definition: A first or preliminary version of a device or vehicle.
etymology: From Greek prototypon, from proto- 'first' plus typos 'pattern.'
exampleSentence: The prototype wobbled, but the team could see how the final design would work.

definition: A manifestation or embodiment, often in digital form.
etymology: From Sanskrit avatara 'descent,' from ava- 'down' plus tarati 'crosses over,' originally a god's incarnation.
exampleSentence: His online avatar is a small purple frog with sunglasses.

definition: A perfect example of a quality or type.
etymology: From Greek epitome 'cutting short,' from epi- plus temnein 'to cut.'
exampleSentence: He is the epitome of dad-joke energy at every barbecue.

definition: A model of excellence.
etymology: From Old Italian paragone 'touchstone,' from Greek parakonein 'to sharpen.'
exampleSentence: Their team lead is widely regarded as a paragon of patience.

definition: A typical or excellent example.
etymology: From Latin exemplar 'model,' from exemplum 'sample.'
exampleSentence: The chapel is held up as an exemplar of late Gothic design.

definition: The most perfect or typical example of a quality.
etymology: From Medieval Latin quinta essentia 'fifth essence,' the substance that medieval philosophers believed composed heavenly bodies.
exampleSentence: That diner is the quintessence of small-town breakfast.

definition: The highest or culminating point of development.
etymology: From Greek apotheosis 'deification,' from apo- plus theos 'god.'
exampleSentence: His final film was widely seen as the apotheosis of the genre.

definition: The highest point of achievement.
etymology: From Greek akme 'peak, prime,' from ake 'point.'
exampleSentence: That album was the acme of his short, sharp career.

definition: The highest point reached by a celestial or other object; the time of greatest power.
etymology: From Arabic samt ar-ras 'path above the head,' via Old French.
exampleSentence: The team reached its zenith just before half the roster left in free agency.

definition: The lowest point.
etymology: From Arabic nazir 'opposite,' specifically nazir as-samt 'opposite the zenith.'
exampleSentence: That bad gig in a basement was the nadir of his comedy career.

definition: The most successful point.
etymology: From Late Latin pinnaculum, from pinna 'point.'
exampleSentence: Winning the championship at thirty-six was the pinnacle of her career.

definition: The highest or climactic point of something.
etymology: From Late Latin culminatio, from culminare 'to crown,' from culmen 'summit.'
exampleSentence: The festival is the culmination of months of village preparation.

definition: A gradual increase in loudness or intensity.
etymology: From Italian crescendo 'growing,' gerund of crescere 'to grow,' from Latin crescere.
exampleSentence: The argument built to a crescendo before her dad called everyone for dinner.

definition: To criticize unfairly or to disparage.
etymology: From Latin denigratus, past participle of denigrare 'to blacken,' from de- plus nigrare 'to make black.'
exampleSentence: He denigrated the new hire's resume in front of the whole team.

definition: To express disapproval of.
etymology: From Latin deprecatus, past participle of deprecari 'to pray against, ward off,' from de- plus precari 'to pray.'
exampleSentence: Engineers deprecated the old endpoint while quietly leaving it running.

definition: To regard or speak of as being of little worth.
etymology: From Old French desparagier 'to marry someone unequal,' from des- plus parage 'equal rank.'
exampleSentence: It does no good to disparage your competition during a sales call.

definition: To make someone or something seem unimportant.
etymology: Coined by Thomas Jefferson in 1782, from be- plus little.
exampleSentence: He had a habit of belittling his teammates' contributions in meetings.

definition: To express contempt for; to ridicule.
etymology: From Latin deridere 'to laugh at,' from de- plus ridere 'to laugh.'
exampleSentence: Critics derided the building's exterior until the interior won them over.

definition: To publicly criticize by using ridicule.
etymology: From French lampon, possibly from lampons 'let us drink,' a refrain in seventeenth-century drinking songs.
exampleSentence: The sketch show lampooned every politician in the state by week's end.

definition: The use of humor or irony to expose folly.
etymology: From Latin satura 'medley,' originally a kind of poetic miscellany.
exampleSentence: Half the audience didn't realize the article was satire.

definition: An imitation that exaggerates for comic effect.
etymology: From Greek paroidia 'mock-song,' from para- plus oide 'song.'
exampleSentence: The film opens with a parody of a corporate motivational video.

definition: A work that imitates the style of another, often in a complimentary way.
etymology: From French pastiche, from Italian pasticcio 'pie, hodgepodge.'
exampleSentence: Her album is a loving pastiche of seventies disco.

definition: A picture or description that exaggerates features for comic effect.
etymology: From Italian caricatura 'exaggeration,' from caricare 'to load, exaggerate.'
exampleSentence: His sketch was a fond caricature of the school principal.

definition: The expression of meaning through language that signifies the opposite.
etymology: From Greek eironeia 'dissimulation,' from eiron 'one who feigns ignorance.'
exampleSentence: It is not lost on him that the fire chief's house caught fire from a candle.

definition: The use of irony to mock or convey contempt.
etymology: From Greek sarkasmos, from sarkazein 'to tear flesh,' from sarx 'flesh.'
exampleSentence: Her email was technically polite but the sarcasm was loud.

definition: A mild word used in place of a harsh one.
etymology: From Greek euphemismos, from eu- 'well' plus pheme 'speech.'
exampleSentence: 'Right-sizing' is corporate euphemism for layoffs.

definition: A derogatory term used in place of a neutral one.
etymology: From Greek dys- 'bad' plus pheme 'speech,' modeled on euphemism.
