exampleSentence: Calling a thoughtful film 'a snooze' is dysphemism dressed as criticism.

definition: Exaggerated statements not meant to be taken literally.
etymology: From Greek hyperbole 'excess,' from hyper- plus ballein 'to throw.'
exampleSentence: Saying he died of embarrassment is hyperbole, but only just.

definition: Ironic understatement that affirms by negating its opposite.
etymology: From Greek litotes 'plainness,' from litos 'plain.'
exampleSentence: Calling the storm 'not exactly mild' is textbook litotes.

definition: The use of a related term to refer to something else.
etymology: From Greek metonymia 'change of name,' from meta- plus onoma 'name.'
exampleSentence: Using 'the White House' to mean the administration is metonymy.

definition: A figure of speech in which a part stands for the whole.
etymology: From Greek synekdokhe 'taking together,' from syn- plus ekdokhe 'interpretation.'
exampleSentence: Saying 'wheels' for 'car' is synecdoche.

definition: A figure of speech combining contradictory terms.
etymology: From Greek oxymoron, from oxys 'sharp' plus moros 'dull.'
exampleSentence: He muttered the usual oxymoron about jumbo shrimp.

definition: A statement that contradicts itself yet may be true.
etymology: From Greek paradoxon 'contrary opinion,' from para- 'contrary' plus doxa 'opinion.'
exampleSentence: The paradox is that working harder sometimes produces less.

definition: A person or thing that is the direct opposite of another.
etymology: From Greek antithesis 'opposition,' from anti- plus tithenai 'to set.'
exampleSentence: He was, in every respect, the antithesis of his older brother.

definition: To divide into sharply contrasting groups.
etymology: From French polariser, from pole, from Latin polus, from Greek polos 'pivot.'
exampleSentence: The proposal polarized even the usually quiet members of the council.

definition: To shock or excite into action.
etymology: From the experiments of Luigi Galvani, the eighteenth-century Italian who passed electric currents through frog legs.
exampleSentence: A surprise visit from the founder galvanized the team.

definition: To cause or accelerate a change.
etymology: From Greek katalysis 'dissolution,' from kata- plus lysis 'a loosening,' a chemistry term extended to social change.
exampleSentence: A single article catalyzed protests in three cities.

definition: To cause something, often bad, to happen suddenly.
etymology: From Latin praecipitatus, past participle of praecipitare 'to throw headlong,' from praeceps 'headfirst.'
exampleSentence: His resignation precipitated a small crisis at the magazine.

definition: To instigate or stir up an undesirable sentiment or action.
etymology: From Latin fomentum 'warm application,' from fovere 'to warm,' originally a medical term for warming inflamed parts.
exampleSentence: Outside actors fomented unrest by spreading half-true rumors.

definition: To encourage or stir up violent or unlawful behavior.
etymology: From Latin incitare 'to put in motion,' from in- plus citare 'to stir up.'
exampleSentence: The speech was designed to incite the crowd, and it did.

definition: To bring about by incitement.
etymology: From Latin instigatus, past participle of instigare 'to urge on.'
exampleSentence: She instigated the prank, though she never actually threw a single water balloon.

definition: To stir up public concern or interest about an issue.
etymology: From Latin agitatus, past participle of agitare 'to set in motion,' frequentative of agere.
exampleSentence: She agitated for sidewalk repairs until the city finally relented.

definition: To make uneasy or embarrassed.
etymology: From Old French desconfit, past participle of desconfire 'to defeat,' from des- plus confire 'to make.'
exampleSentence: A surprise question about his sources discomfited the witness.

definition: To disturb the composure of.
etymology: From obsolete French disconcerter, from dis- plus concerter 'to harmonize.'
exampleSentence: The microphone feedback briefly disconcerted the otherwise polished speaker.

definition: To make anxious or unsettled.
etymology: From Latin perturbare 'to confuse,' from per- plus turbare 'to disturb.'
exampleSentence: The strange noise from the engine perturbed her for the rest of the drive.

definition: To bewilder or perplex.
etymology: Of uncertain English dialect origin, possibly from 'flummock' meaning to bewilder, first attested in the mid nineteenth century.
exampleSentence: The tax form flummoxed her on page one.

definition: To confuse or disconcert.
etymology: A nineteenth-century American jocular alteration of words like discompose or discombobricate.
exampleSentence: Three time-zone changes in two days will discombobulate anyone.

definition: To so surprise or confuse as to render speechless.
etymology: From Latin non plus 'no more,' the point beyond which one cannot proceed.
exampleSentence: His one-word answer nonplussed the panel.

definition: To cause surprise or confusion.
etymology: From Old French confondre, from Latin confundere 'to pour together,' from con- plus fundere 'to pour.'
exampleSentence: The data confounded everyone's predictions for the third quarter in a row.

definition: To cause to become confused.
etymology: From English be- plus wilder 'to lead astray,' related to wilderness.
exampleSentence: The new shopping center's signage bewildered even longtime locals.

definition: To make someone unable to think clearly.
etymology: From Latin perplexus 'entangled,' from per- plus plectere 'to plait.'
exampleSentence: The riddle perplexed her until she gave up and asked for a hint.

definition: Slow to understand; or annoyingly imperceptive.
etymology: From Latin obtusus 'dulled,' past participle of obtundere 'to beat against,' from ob- plus tundere 'to beat.'
exampleSentence: He's not obtuse, just stubborn about admitting he's wrong.

definition: Not feeling or showing emotion.
etymology: From in- 'not' plus Latin passivus 'capable of feeling,' from pati 'to suffer.'
exampleSentence: He sat impassive while the witness described the morning of the fire.

definition: Impossible to understand or interpret.
etymology: From Late Latin inscrutabilis, from in- plus scrutari 'to search.'
exampleSentence: Her inscrutable smile gave away nothing about the verdict.

definition: Difficult to interpret or understand; mysterious.
etymology: From Latin aenigma, from Greek ainigma 'riddle,' from ainissesthai 'to speak in riddles.'
exampleSentence: His enigmatic emails left the team guessing about the deadline.

definition: Having a meaning that is mysterious or obscure.
etymology: From Greek kryptikos 'hidden,' from kryptos 'hidden.'
exampleSentence: He sent a cryptic text at midnight that nobody could decipher.

definition: Not expressed directly.
etymology: From Latin obliquus 'slanting,' of uncertain origin.
exampleSentence: He gave an oblique reference to the layoffs but refused to confirm them.

definition: Concise and forceful in expression.
etymology: From Middle English pith, from Old English pitha 'central core of a stem,' used figuratively for the essential point.
exampleSentence: The professor was famous for pithy comments scribbled in red ink.

definition: Deserving praise and commendation.
etymology: From Latin laudabilis, from laudare 'to praise,' from laus 'praise.'
exampleSentence: Her laudable effort to learn three new languages in a year fizzled by April.

definition: Expressing praise.
etymology: From Latin laudatorius, from laudare 'to praise.'
exampleSentence: The review was laudatory in places and devastating in others.

definition: Apparently attractive but having no real value.
etymology: From Latin meretricius 'of a prostitute,' from meretrix 'prostitute,' from merere 'to earn.'
exampleSentence: The campaign's promises were meretricious at best.

definition: Loud, mournful, and resonant.
etymology: From Latin plangens, present participle of plangere 'to lament, beat one's breast.'
exampleSentence: The plangent foghorn carried for miles along the coast.

definition: A soft, whispering or rustling sound.
etymology: From Latin susurrus 'a whisper.'
exampleSentence: A susurrus of leaves followed her down the empty path.

definition: A harsh mixture of sounds.
etymology: From Greek kakophonia, from kakos 'bad' plus phone 'sound.'
exampleSentence: A cacophony of car horns greeted the green light.

definition: The pleasant quality of sounds.
etymology: From Greek euphonia, from eu- 'good' plus phone 'sound.'
exampleSentence: The choir achieved a euphony you could feel in your chest.

definition: Sweet or musical; pleasant to hear.
etymology: From Late Latin mellifluus, from Latin mel 'honey' plus fluere 'to flow.'
exampleSentence: His mellifluous voice made even the weather report soothing.

definition: Sweet and soothing, especially of sound.
etymology: From Old French doucet, diminutive of doux 'sweet,' from Latin dulcis.
exampleSentence: Her dulcet tones could not disguise the harsh content of the message.

definition: Loud and harsh.
etymology: From Latin stridens, present participle of stridere 'to creak.'
exampleSentence: He took a more strident tone in the second half of the debate.

definition: Making a disturbingly loud, unpleasant noise.
etymology: From Latin raucus 'hoarse.'
exampleSentence: The raucous after-party drew the attention of every neighbor on the block.

definition: A loud and confused noise; a vehement public outcry.
etymology: From Latin clamor 'a shout,' from clamare 'to shout.'
exampleSentence: There was a clamor for the manager's resignation by lunchtime.

definition: A loud, unpleasant, and prolonged noise.
etymology: From Old English dyne, related to Sanskrit dhuni 'roaring.'
exampleSentence: You could barely hear yourself think over the din of construction.

definition: A chaotic noise caused by a crowd.
etymology: Of uncertain origin, possibly from a Gaelic exclamation, first attested in English in the sixteenth century.
exampleSentence: The hubbub in the cafe died down only when the espresso machine broke.

definition: A loud, confused noise, especially one caused by a large mass of people.
etymology: From Latin tumultus 'an uproar.'
exampleSentence: The tumult on the trading floor stopped the moment the bell rang.

definition: A state of great disturbance or uncertainty.
etymology: Of obscure sixteenth-century English origin, possibly an alteration of older words for confusion.
exampleSentence: The startup was in turmoil after both founders resigned.

definition: Wild and noisy disorder.
etymology: From Greek pan- 'all' plus daimon 'demon,' coined by John Milton in Paradise Lost as the capital of hell.
exampleSentence: It was pandemonium in the green room after the surprise win.

definition: A confused fight or scuffle.
etymology: From French melee, from Old French meslee 'mixture,' past participle of mesler 'to mix.'
exampleSentence: A bench-clearing melee delayed the game by twenty minutes.

definition: A noisy disturbance or quarrel.
etymology: From French fracas, from Italian fracasso 'crash,' from fracassare 'to smash.'
exampleSentence: The minor fracas at the bar somehow made the local paper.

definition: A minor disagreement or accident.
etymology: From French contretemps 'wrong time,' from contre- 'against' plus temps 'time.'
exampleSentence: They had a brief contretemps over who was paying for parking.

definition: A confusing or embarrassing situation.
etymology: From Italian imbroglio 'a tangle,' from imbrogliare 'to confuse,' from broglio 'intrigue.'
exampleSentence: The diplomatic imbroglio took months to untangle.

definition: A complicated or hazardous situation.
etymology: From English quag 'marsh' plus mire 'swamp,' both Germanic in origin.
exampleSentence: The merger turned into a regulatory quagmire.

definition: A complicated or confused situation.
etymology: From Dutch moeras 'swamp,' from Old French maresc, from Frankish.
exampleSentence: He waded through the morass of paperwork in search of a single date.

definition: A complicated network of passages or a confusing situation.
etymology: From Greek labyrinthos, the mythical maze built by Daedalus on Crete.
exampleSentence: The labyrinth of insurance forms exhausted them long before any care arrived.

definition: A network of small, interconnected passages or rooms.
etymology: From Anglo-French warenne 'reserve,' originally a rabbit enclosure, from a Germanic root meaning to guard.
exampleSentence: The old apartment was a warren of low-ceilinged rooms.

definition: A stronghold or place of refuge.
etymology: From French redoute, from Italian ridotto 'place of retreat,' from Latin reductus 'withdrawn.'
exampleSentence: The library became his redoubt during finals week.

definition: A stronghold or center of resistance.
etymology: From French bastion, from Italian bastione 'fortification,' from bastire 'to build.'
exampleSentence: For decades the magazine was a bastion of careful long-form reporting.

definition: A fortress, typically on high ground, protecting or dominating a city.
etymology: From Italian cittadella, diminutive of citta 'city,' from Latin civitas.
exampleSentence: The old citadel still looks down on the harbor at sunset.

definition: A large nest of a bird of prey built on a high cliff; or a high, secluded place.
etymology: From Medieval Latin aeria, possibly from Old French aire 'family nest,' or from Latin area 'open space.'
exampleSentence: From his glass-walled aerie, the CEO had a view of three states.

definition: A sacred or private place.
etymology: From Latin sanctum 'holy place,' neuter of sanctus 'holy.'
exampleSentence: His tiny basement workshop was a sanctum no one else dared enter.

definition: Honored as holy.
etymology: From Old English halgian 'to make holy,' from halig 'holy.'
exampleSentence: The diamond at Yankee Stadium is hallowed ground for fans of a certain age.

definition: Accorded respect because of age, wisdom, or character.
etymology: From Latin venerabilis, from venerari 'to revere,' from venus 'love, charm.'
exampleSentence: The venerable scholar refused to retire because the email was finally working.

definition: A person of profound wisdom.
etymology: From Old French sage 'wise,' from Vulgar Latin sapius, from Latin sapere 'to be wise.'
exampleSentence: In her later years she became a kind of neighborhood sage for new parents.

definition: A learned expert or commentator on a subject.
etymology: From Sanskrit pandita 'learned one,' originally referring to Hindu scholars.
exampleSentence: Every pundit had a different theory about the surprise resignation.

definition: A learned person, especially a distinguished scientist.
etymology: From French savant, present participle of savoir 'to know,' from Latin sapere 'to be wise.'
exampleSentence: The chess savant could play four games at once while reading a novel.

definition: A person who inspires others through brilliance or eminence.
etymology: From Latin luminarium 'lamp,' from lumen 'light.'
exampleSentence: Several literary luminaries gave readings at the small bookstore.

definition: A young person with exceptional abilities.
etymology: From Latin prodigium 'omen, marvel,' originally referring to extraordinary natural signs.
exampleSentence: The violin prodigy played her first concerto at age six.

definition: A person of wide-ranging knowledge or learning.
etymology: From Greek polymathes 'having learned much,' from poly- plus manthanein 'to learn.'
exampleSentence: Leonardo da Vinci is the textbook polymath.

definition: A skilled storyteller.
etymology: From French raconteur, from raconter 'to recount,' from re- plus aconter 'to count, relate.'
exampleSentence: Her uncle was the family raconteur, with a story for every dish on the table.

definition: A person who enjoys good food, drink, and social pleasures.
etymology: From French bon 'good' plus vivant 'living,' present participle of vivre 'to live.'
exampleSentence: A self-described bon vivant, he could recommend the best bistro in any city.

definition: An expert judge in matters of taste.
etymology: From Old French connoisseor, from connoistre 'to know,' from Latin cognoscere.
exampleSentence: He was a connoisseur of obscure cheeses and obscure jokes alike.

definition: A passionate enthusiast and devotee.
etymology: From Spanish aficionado 'fan,' past participle of aficionar 'to inspire affection,' from afecto 'affection.'
exampleSentence: As an aficionado of vintage Vespas, he knew every paint code by heart.

definition: A person devoted to a cause or pursuit.
etymology: From French devot, from Latin devotus 'devoted,' past participle of devovere.
exampleSentence: She is a longtime devotee of cold-water swimming, even in January.

definition: A devoted assistant or follower.
etymology: From Greek akolouthos 'follower,' originally a church assistant.
exampleSentence: A small group of acolytes followed her chef training program across the country.

definition: A follower or student of a teacher or leader.
etymology: From Latin discipulus 'student,' from discere 'to learn.'
exampleSentence: His earliest disciples are now department chairs at three different universities.

definition: A person guided and supported by an experienced or influential mentor.
etymology: From French protege, past participle of proteger 'to protect,' from Latin protegere.
exampleSentence: Her protege opened a competing restaurant down the street, with her blessing.

definition: An experienced and trusted adviser.
etymology: After Mentor, the wise adviser of Odysseus's son in Homer's Odyssey.
exampleSentence: Every new associate is paired with a mentor for the first six months.

definition: A person who gives money or other help.
etymology: From Late Latin benefactor, from benefacere 'to do good,' from bene 'well' plus facere 'to do.'
exampleSentence: An anonymous benefactor paid the school's heating bill that winter.

definition: A person who gives financial or other support to a person or cause.
etymology: From Old French patron 'master, defender,' from Latin patronus, from pater 'father.'
exampleSentence: The Medici were patrons of artists who needed both gold and protection.

definition: Well meaning and kindly.
etymology: From Latin benevolens, from bene 'well' plus velle 'to wish.'
exampleSentence: Her benevolent uncle was the reason any of them finished college.

definition: Wishing evil or harm to others.
etymology: From Latin malevolens, from male 'badly' plus velle 'to wish.'
exampleSentence: The villain has a strangely malevolent laugh that the children find hilarious.

definition: Doing good or causing good to be done.
etymology: From Latin beneficens, from bene 'well' plus facere 'to do.'
exampleSentence: His beneficent grandmother left a fund for any cousin who wanted to travel.

definition: Causing harm or destruction.
etymology: From Latin maleficens, from male 'badly' plus facere 'to do.'
exampleSentence: In the story, a maleficent witch turns the well to ink.

definition: Wicked or criminal.
etymology: From Latin nefarius, from nefas 'crime,' from ne- 'not' plus fas 'right, lawful.'
exampleSentence: He was caught up in a nefarious scheme involving used phones and ferry tickets.

definition: Proceeding in a gradual, subtle way with harmful effects.
etymology: From Latin insidiosus 'cunning,' from insidiae 'ambush,' from insidere 'to sit in wait.'
exampleSentence: The insidious leak destroyed the floor before anyone noticed water at all.

definition: Extremely unpleasant; repulsive.
etymology: From Latin odiosus, from odium 'hatred.'
exampleSentence: He has the odious habit of clipping his nails during conference calls.

definition: Inspiring disgust and loathing.
etymology: From Latin abhorrens, present participle of abhorrere 'to shrink from,' from ab- plus horrere 'to bristle.'
exampleSentence: The new policy was abhorrent to anyone who'd actually worked the night shift.

definition: Extremely distasteful; unacceptable.
etymology: From Latin repugnans, present participle of repugnare 'to fight against,' from re- plus pugnare 'to fight.'
exampleSentence: The very idea of charging admission to the playground was repugnant to him.

definition: Causing moral revulsion.
etymology: From Latin abominabilis, from abominari 'to deprecate as an ill omen,' from ab- plus omen.
exampleSentence: The hotel's coffee was abominable, but the view made up for it.

definition: Extremely bad or unpleasant.
etymology: From Latin execrabilis, from execrari 'to curse,' from ex- plus sacer 'sacred.'
exampleSentence: His execrable handwriting forced the bank to call him for confirmation.

definition: Causing harm or damage.
etymology: From Greek deleterios 'destructive,' from deleter 'destroyer,' from deleisthai 'to hurt.'
exampleSentence: Long hours had a deleterious effect on the team's creativity.

definition: Causing or likely to cause damage or harm.
etymology: From Latin injuriosus, from injuria 'wrong,' from in- plus jus 'right.'
exampleSentence: He claimed the article was injurious to his professional reputation.

definition: Threatening harm; menacing.
etymology: From Old English bealuful, from bealu 'evil' plus -ful.
exampleSentence: The dog gave the mail carrier a baleful stare from the window.

definition: Causing harm, ruin, or death.
etymology: From Old English bana 'slayer' plus -ful, related to Old Norse bani 'death.'
exampleSentence: The baneful effects of the drought were felt for years after the rains returned.

definition: Harmful, poisonous, or unpleasant.
etymology: From Latin noxius, from noxa 'harm.'
exampleSentence: A noxious fume drifted out of the chemistry lab and into the hall.

definition: Poisonous; very harmful or unpleasant.
etymology: From Late Latin toxicus 'poisoned,' from Latin toxicum 'poison,' from Greek toxikon 'arrow poison.'
exampleSentence: The toxic work environment finally drove three managers to quit on the same day.

definition: Extremely severe or harmful; bitterly hostile.
etymology: From Latin virulentus, from virus 'poison.'
exampleSentence: He launched a virulent attack on the new editor in his weekly column.

definition: Having an irritatingly strong taste or smell; angry and bitter.
etymology: From Latin acer 'sharp,' altered on analogy with acid.
exampleSentence: An acrid haze hung over the city for days after the wildfire.

definition: Having a sharply strong taste or smell.
etymology: From Latin pungens, present participle of pungere 'to prick.'
exampleSentence: A pungent garlic broth filled the entire apartment.

definition: Strongly reminiscent or suggestive of something; fragrant.
etymology: From Latin redolens, present participle of redolere 'to give off a scent,' from re- plus olere 'to smell.'
exampleSentence: The kitchen was redolent of cinnamon and slightly burnt toast.

definition: Relating to the sense of smell.
etymology: From Latin olfactus 'smell,' past participle of olfacere 'to smell out.'
exampleSentence: Old bookstores have an olfactory signature no candle has captured.

definition: Relating to the sense of taste.
etymology: From Latin gustare 'to taste.'
exampleSentence: The pop-up promised a gustatory tour of West African cuisine.

definition: A person's appreciation of taste and flavor.
etymology: From Latin palatum 'roof of the mouth,' once thought to be the seat of taste.
exampleSentence: Years of tasting wine had given her a refined palate and a permanent stain on the tablecloth.

definition: A lover or connoisseur of wine.
etymology: From Greek oinos 'wine' plus -phile 'lover of.'
exampleSentence: As a serious oenophile, he treated even three-dollar wine with patient respect.

definition: A person who enjoys eating, sometimes to excess.
etymology: From Old French gourmant 'glutton,' of uncertain ultimate origin.
exampleSentence: The famous gourmand wrote about every meal as if it were the last.

definition: A connoisseur of fine food and drink.
etymology: From French gourmet, alteration of Old French groume 'wine-taster's servant.'
exampleSentence: The gourmet pretended he could taste the difference, and maybe he could.

definition: Excessively greedy, especially for food.
etymology: From Latin gluto 'glutton,' from gluttire 'to swallow.'
exampleSentence: His gluttonous afternoon at the buffet had consequences he didn't anticipate.

definition: Extremely hungry.
etymology: From Old French ravineux 'voracious,' from raviner 'to ravage.'
exampleSentence: After the hike we were all ravenous, even the picky teenager.

definition: Extremely hungry.
etymology: From Old French faim 'hunger,' from Latin fames 'hunger.'
exampleSentence: He arrived at the dinner party famished and slightly embarrassed about it.

definition: To satisfy a desire or appetite fully.
etymology: From Latin satiatus, past participle of satiare 'to satisfy,' from satis 'enough.'
exampleSentence: Three helpings of pasta finally satiated even the teenager.

definition: To satisfy a thirst or desire.
etymology: From Old English slacian 'to become slack,' related to slæc 'slack.'
exampleSentence: Nothing slakes a thirst quite like ice water after a long run.

definition: To satisfy thirst or extinguish a fire.
etymology: From Old English acwencan 'to extinguish.'
exampleSentence: The fountain in the plaza was always full of dogs trying to quench their thirst.

definition: To drink, or to absorb information.
etymology: From Latin imbibere 'to drink in,' from in- plus bibere 'to drink.'
exampleSentence: He liked to imbibe his morning podcast along with his coffee.

definition: A drink poured as an offering, or, jokingly, a drink in general.
etymology: From Latin libatio, from libare 'to pour an offering,' originally a religious term.
exampleSentence: He raised his libation to the bartender and to the slow Friday afternoon.

definition: A thing presented as an offering, especially to a deity.
etymology: From Late Latin oblatio, from offerre 'to offer,' from ob- plus ferre 'to bring.'
exampleSentence: The small loaf of bread at the altar served as an oblation of thanks.

definition: A religious ceremony regarded as imparting divine grace.
etymology: From Latin sacramentum 'solemn oath,' from sacrare 'to consecrate.'
exampleSentence: For her grandmother, Sunday breakfast was practically a sacrament.

definition: A set form of public religious worship.
etymology: From Greek leitourgia 'public service,' from leitos 'public' plus -ergos 'working.'
exampleSentence: He could recite the entire liturgy from memory but never raised his voice in song.

definition: A principle laid down by an authority as unquestionably true.
etymology: From Greek dogma 'opinion,' from dokein 'to seem good.'
exampleSentence: She refused to accept the company's onboarding dogma without asking why.

definition: Belief or opinion contrary to orthodox doctrine.
etymology: From Greek hairesis 'choice, sect,' from hairein 'to choose.'
exampleSentence: Suggesting that pineapple belongs on pizza is heresy in his household.

definition: Not conforming with accepted standards or beliefs.
etymology: From Greek heterodoxos, from heteros 'other' plus doxa 'opinion.'
exampleSentence: His heterodox views on monetary policy got him uninvited from two conferences.

definition: Following established or traditional doctrines or rules.
etymology: From Greek orthodoxos, from orthos 'right' plus doxa 'opinion.'
exampleSentence: An orthodox approach to the recipe means no shortcuts on the broth.

definition: A person who attacks cherished beliefs or institutions.
etymology: From Medieval Greek eikonoklastes, from eikon 'image' plus klan 'to break,' originally an image-breaker in religious disputes.
exampleSentence: He was the iconoclast every faculty meeting needed.

definition: An unorthodox or independent-minded person.
etymology: After Samuel A. Maverick, a nineteenth-century Texas rancher who refused to brand his cattle.
exampleSentence: The team's resident maverick eventually founded a competing studio.

definition: A person whose behavior or views do not conform to prevailing norms.
etymology: From English non- plus conformist, originally a seventeenth-century term for English Protestants who refused to conform to the Church of England.
exampleSentence: Even as a child she was a nonconformist about every uniform requirement.

definition: A person who deserts a cause or organization.
etymology: From Spanish renegado 'apostate,' from Medieval Latin renegatus, past participle of renegare 'to deny.'
exampleSentence: A handful of renegade engineers left to start their own company.

definition: A person who renounces a religious or political belief.
etymology: From Late Latin apostata, from Greek apostates 'rebel,' from apostenai 'to defect.'
exampleSentence: He was branded an apostate by his old colleagues at the foundation.

definition: An outcast.
etymology: From Tamil paraiyar, plural of paraiyan, the name of a low caste of drummers in southern India.
exampleSentence: After the scandal, he was a pariah at the country club for nearly a year.

definition: A person rejected by society.
etymology: From Middle English out- plus cast, past participle of casten 'to throw,' from Old Norse kasta.
exampleSentence: The book follows an outcast who eventually leads the rebellion he was blamed for.

definition: Not able to be touched or affected; or unrivaled.
etymology: From English un- plus touchable, from touch, from Old French tochier.
exampleSentence: Her record in the hundred meters seemed untouchable for almost a decade.

definition: Without flaw.
etymology: From Latin impeccabilis, from in- plus peccare 'to sin.'
exampleSentence: His impeccable shoes were the first thing anyone noticed.

definition: Without imperfection.
etymology: From English flaw, of Old Norse origin, plus -less.
exampleSentence: Her flawless delivery of the speech impressed even her toughest professor.

definition: In its original condition; unspoiled.
etymology: From Latin pristinus 'former, original.'
exampleSentence: The vinyl, kept in its original sleeve, was in pristine condition.

definition: Perfectly clean and tidy; free from flaws.
etymology: From Latin immaculatus, from in- plus macula 'spot, stain.'
exampleSentence: He kept his garage immaculate as a matter of personal religion.

definition: Free from any imperfection or fault.
etymology: From English un- plus blemish, from Old French blesmir 'to make pale, injure.'
exampleSentence: Her unblemished record finally took a hit on her thirteenth season.

definition: Damaged or tarnished, especially morally.
etymology: From English sully, from Old French souillier 'to soil,' from sou 'pig.'
exampleSentence: He felt his reputation had been sullied by association with the scandal.

definition: To damage the reputation of.
etymology: From English be- plus smirch 'to dirty,' of uncertain origin.
exampleSentence: Anonymous comments online tried to besmirch the candidate's record.

definition: To make something less valuable or respected; or to dull the surface of metal.
etymology: From Old French ternir 'to dim,' from terne 'dull.'
exampleSentence: The scandal tarnished what had been a quietly successful career.

definition: To weaken or damage.
etymology: From Old French empeirier 'to make worse,' from Late Latin impejorare, from in- plus pejor 'worse.'
exampleSentence: A bad night of sleep can impair judgment more than a glass of wine.

definition: To spoil or impair the quality or efficiency of.
etymology: From Latin vitiatus, past participle of vitiare 'to spoil,' from vitium 'fault.'
exampleSentence: A single typo vitiated the contract and required a full redraft.

definition: To erode the base or foundation of; to weaken gradually.
etymology: From Old English under plus minen 'to mine,' from Old French miner.
exampleSentence: Constant micromanagement undermined the team's confidence.

definition: To undermine the power and authority of an established system.
etymology: From Latin subvertere 'to overturn,' from sub- plus vertere 'to turn.'
exampleSentence: The play subverts every expectation about courtroom drama in act two.

definition: To deliberately destroy or obstruct.
etymology: From French sabotage, from sabot 'wooden shoe,' allegedly from disgruntled workers throwing shoes into machinery.
exampleSentence: He suspected someone had sabotaged the demo before his big pitch.

definition: To prevent someone from accomplishing something.
etymology: From Old Norse thvert 'across,' originally an adverb meaning crosswise.
exampleSentence: The weather thwarted three different attempts at the summit.

definition: To remove a need or difficulty.
etymology: From Latin obviatus, past participle of obviare 'to meet, prevent,' from ob- plus via 'way.'
exampleSentence: A short phone call obviated the need for a whole afternoon of emails.

definition: To take action to prevent an anticipated event.
etymology: From English pre- plus Latin emere 'to buy,' originally meaning to acquire by right beforehand.
exampleSentence: She preempted the inevitable question with a slide already on the screen.

definition: To prevent by taking action in advance.
etymology: From Old English foresteall 'ambush,' from fore- 'in front' plus steall 'position.'
exampleSentence: He forestalled criticism by acknowledging the bug in his opening sentence.

definition: To shorten by cutting off a part.
etymology: From Latin truncatus, past participle of truncare 'to lop off,' from truncus 'trunk.'
exampleSentence: They had to truncate the panel discussion when the fire alarm went off.

definition: To shorten a piece of writing without losing its sense.
etymology: From Old French abregier 'to shorten,' from Late Latin abbreviare, from ad- plus brevis 'short.'
exampleSentence: The publisher decided to abridge the novel for younger readers.

definition: To make denser or more concise.
etymology: From Latin condensare 'to make dense,' from con- plus densare 'to thicken.'
exampleSentence: She managed to condense the whole proposal into a single thoughtful paragraph.

definition: To shorten a word, phrase, or text.
etymology: From Late Latin abbreviatus, past participle of abbreviare 'to shorten,' from ad- plus brevis 'short.'
exampleSentence: He abbreviates every text message into near-illegible shorthand.

definition: To prolong; to extend in time.
etymology: From Latin protractus, past participle of protrahere 'to draw out,' from pro- plus trahere 'to draw.'
exampleSentence: The senator protracted the debate well past midnight with carefully composed questions.

definition: To make something last longer.
etymology: From Late Latin prolongare, from pro- plus longus 'long.'
exampleSentence: They prolonged the goodbye until it became its own little event.

definition: Tediously lengthy.
etymology: From Latin prolixus 'extended,' from pro- plus liquere 'to flow.'
exampleSentence: His prolix introduction lost the audience before the keynote even began.

definition: Using more words than needed.
etymology: From Latin verbosus 'wordy,' from verbum 'word.'
exampleSentence: A verbose email is often a sign of an unclear thought.

definition: Sparing in the use of words; abrupt.
etymology: From Latin tersus 'polished,' past participle of tergere 'to wipe.'
exampleSentence: His terse reply confirmed her suspicion that he was furious.

definition: Abrupt or offhand in manner.
etymology: From French brusque, from Italian brusco 'sharp, tart,' originally describing a kind of stinging shrub.
exampleSentence: The brusque receptionist hung up before she could finish the question.

definition: Rudely brief.
etymology: From Latin curtus 'short.'
exampleSentence: A curt 'fine' was the only answer she got at dinner.

definition: Not revealing one's thoughts or feelings readily.
etymology: From Latin reticens, present participle of reticere 'to keep silent,' from re- plus tacere 'to be silent.'
exampleSentence: He was reticent about his childhood but generous about everything else.

definition: Modest or shy because of a lack of self-confidence.
etymology: From Latin diffidens, present participle of diffidere 'to mistrust,' from dis- plus fidere 'to trust.'
exampleSentence: The diffident new hire eventually became the loudest voice in standup.

definition: Showing or suffering from nervousness or fear.
etymology: From Old French temoros, from Latin timor 'fear.'
exampleSentence: A timorous knock at the door turned out to be the building inspector.

definition: Contemptibly lacking in courage.
etymology: From Middle English crauen 'to crave,' though traditionally linked to craven 'defeated,' of disputed origin.
exampleSentence: His craven response to the scandal cost him the last of his allies.

definition: Showing a lack of courage or determination.
etymology: From Late Latin pusillanimis, from pusillus 'very small' plus animus 'mind.'
exampleSentence: Their pusillanimous statement managed to take no side at all.

definition: Whining or complaining in a feeble way.
etymology: From English snivel, from Old English snyflan 'to run at the nose.'
exampleSentence: The sniveling apology made everything worse, not better.

definition: Excessively flattering or ingratiating.
etymology: From Medieval Latin unctuosus 'oily,' from Latin unctus 'anointing.'
exampleSentence: His unctuous compliments made even the recipients uncomfortable.

definition: Oily or greasy; or excessively flattering.
etymology: From Latin oleaginus 'of the olive,' from olea 'olive.'
exampleSentence: The oleaginous salesman knew every customer's birthday and weakness.

definition: Excessively sweet or sentimental.
etymology: From Medieval Latin saccharum 'sugar,' from Greek sakkharon, from Sanskrit sharkara.
exampleSentence: The film's saccharine ending undermined an otherwise sharp script.

definition: Self-pityingly or tearfully sentimental.
etymology: From Middle English Maudeleyne, the form of Mary Magdalene's name, who was depicted tearfully repenting.
exampleSentence: After two beers he became maudlin about his old college roommates.

definition: Sentimental in a feeble way.
etymology: From Middle English mawke 'maggot,' originally meaning loathsome.
exampleSentence: The greeting card aisle is a tour of mawkish prose.

definition: Excessively quaint or sentimental.
etymology: From English baby talk for sweet, attested from the early twentieth century.
exampleSentence: The cafe was almost too twee, with its bunting and tiny mismatched teacups.

definition: Naive, simplistic, and superficial.
etymology: From Latin jejunus 'meager, fasting,' originally referring to an empty stomach.
exampleSentence: His jejune analysis of the budget missed everything that mattered.

definition: Given to moralizing in a pompous way.
etymology: From Latin sententiosus, from sententia 'opinion, maxim.'
exampleSentence: His sententious dinner-table speeches were avoided by the cousins.

definition: Intended to teach, often in a moralizing manner.
etymology: From Greek didaktikos, from didaskein 'to teach.'
exampleSentence: The novel is more didactic than its author seems to realize.

definition: Inclined to lay down principles as if they are incontrovertibly true.
etymology: From Latin dogmaticus, from Greek dogmatikos, from dogma 'opinion.'
exampleSentence: He took a dogmatic stance on every coffee question, including the temperature.

definition: Strongly critical or controversial.
etymology: From Greek polemikos 'warlike,' from polemos 'war.'
exampleSentence: Her polemical essay started three Twitter feuds before lunch.

definition: A person displaying aggressive or exaggerated patriotism or partiality.
etymology: After Nicolas Chauvin, a fictional French soldier known for excessive devotion to Napoleon.
exampleSentence: The team's loudest chauvinist had never actually been to the stadium.

definition: A person with a dislike of foreigners.
etymology: From Greek xenos 'stranger' plus phobos 'fear.'
exampleSentence: He was no xenophobe, but he did insist on his grandmother's recipes.

definition: Extreme patriotism, especially in the form of aggressive foreign policy.
etymology: From the British music-hall refrain 'by jingo,' used in a popular pro-war song in 1877.
exampleSentence: Sports broadcasts that summer felt drenched in cheerful jingoism.

definition: Having a narrow or limited outlook.
etymology: From Late Latin parochialis 'of a parish,' from parochia.
exampleSentence: Her parochial taste in fiction softened after a summer of train travel.

definition: Familiar with and at ease in many different cultures and people.
etymology: From Greek kosmopolites 'citizen of the world,' from kosmos plus polites.
exampleSentence: Her cosmopolitan upbringing meant she could order breakfast in five languages.

definition: Limited in outlook; unsophisticated.
etymology: From Latin provincialis 'of a province,' the Roman term for a region outside the capital.
exampleSentence: He thought of his old hometown's tastes as provincial until he revisited them.
